Arne found the same pattern in eleven other dances: entrances, exits, and lighting changes fall where movement and music realign, rather than at the beginnings of sections of the score. A rehearsal pianist who worked with Strand in the 1960s recalled that she forbade dancers to “listen for the one,” telling them instead to count their own phrases and trust that “the music will find you.” Regularizing the counts, Arne concludes, erased the very feature that organized the dances.

Arne’s theory is a considerable advance, and the company has since restored the original counts in several revivals. Yet the evidence for his claim about breath is much thinner than the evidence for the pattern of convergence. Strand never mentioned breath in her notebooks; the idea derives from a single radio interview in which she said that a phrase should be “as long as it needs to be,” a remark that could as easily refer to dramatic need as to physiological need. Moreover, in at least three of her late works the phrases never realign with the music at all, which suggests that Strand eventually valued the tension of drift for its own sake. Arne’s account explains how many of Strand’s dances are built; why she built them that way remains an open question.

passages.title: Kenning and the Halvey stamp scrip
passages.subject: social-science
passages.text:
In the autumn of 1932, with its two textile mills shut and its only bank closed, the town council of Halvey began paying its employees partly in scrip: paper certificates, redeemable for town taxes, that local merchants agreed to accept for goods. Halvey’s scrip carried an unusual feature. On the back of each certificate were fifty-two squares, and a certificate remained valid only if its holder affixed a one-cent stamp, purchased from the town, to the next empty square each week. In The Fast Dollar (2009), the economic historian Rhoda Kenning argues that this weekly charge, by making it costly to hold scrip, induced residents to spend it quickly, and that the resulting acceleration of exchange explains the revival of Halvey’s retail trade during the eighteen months the scrip circulated.

Kenning’s account has the merit of attending to the design of a currency rather than merely to its quantity, and her reconstruction of the scrip’s circulation from surviving stamp records is ingenious. But she does not clarify what she takes the revival to consist in. At times she points to the number of transactions recorded by Halvey’s merchants, at others to the total value of their sales. Yet the number of transactions could rise sharply even while total sales stagnated, if residents merely broke their purchases into smaller ones in order to pass on scrip before the next stamp came due.

Her argument also assumes that merchants passed scrip on as readily as residents did. Kenning’s own figures suggest otherwise: most certificates returned to the town treasury within a few weeks, tendered by merchants in payment of property taxes. If the scrip traveled mainly from council employees to shopkeepers and back to the treasury, it may have functioned less as a circulating currency than as a means by which the town paid its employees out of future tax receipts—a useful arrangement, but not one that the stamps were needed to produce.

Finally, Kenning does not adequately account for Corley, a town twenty miles downriver that issued scrip in 1933 without any stamp requirement. Records of Corley’s merchants’ association show retail sales there recovering at roughly Halvey’s rate. Kenning dismisses the comparison on the ground that Corley’s economy depended on a railway repair shop that reopened that year. But the reopening of an employer is precisely the kind of factor that could also have contributed to Halvey’s recovery, since one of Halvey’s mills resumed partial operation in the summer of 1933. None of this shows that the stamps were without effect. It suggests, rather, that their effect cannot be read directly from Halvey’s sales figures, and that the town’s experience is better evidence of what a cash-starved municipality can accomplish with its power to tax than of the virtues of money designed to lose value.

passages.title: Apology statutes
passages.subject: law
passages.text:
Passage A

Over the past few decades, many jurisdictions have adopted apology statutes, which prevent a person’s expression of sympathy after an accident or injury from being introduced as evidence of liability in a later lawsuit. Their rationale is straightforward: people, and physicians in particular, would apologize more readily if they did not fear that their words would be used against them, and injured parties who receive apologies would be less inclined to sue. The statutes have been widely praised, yet they rest on uncertain ground.

First, most of them protect only expressions of sympathy (“I am sorry this happened to you”) while leaving admissions of fault fully admissible. They thus encourage precisely the kind of apology that injured people find least satisfying: one that acknowledges suffering but sidesteps responsibility. Such a gesture gives injured people little of what they actually seek, and it may leave them feeling that their injury has been noted rather than answered.

Second, the statutes assume that fear of litigation is what keeps people from apologizing. But when the legal scholar Teodor Brann asked hospital physicians why they had not apologized after a medical error, they cited embarrassment, uncertainty about what had gone wrong, and institutional habit at least as often as legal exposure. A rule of evidence can do nothing about these.

Third, and most troubling, the statutes invite strategic use. An insurer that coaches its policyholders to offer carefully worded, legally weightless expressions of regret may thereby defuse claims that deserve to be pursued, since an injured person who has been soothed is less likely to consult a lawyer. What was meant to make room for moral repair becomes one more instrument for managing liability.

Passage B

Critics of laws that shield apologies from use as evidence sometimes treat any apology made under such protection as suspect, as if regret could be sincere only when it is costly. But sincerity is not measured by legal risk. A driver who says “I’m so sorry” at the scene of a collision may mean it entirely, whether or not the words could later be read to a jury.

It is true that a protected statement of sympathy is not a confession of fault, and some injured people want the latter. But for many, what matters first is acknowledgment of the harm done. In a study by Ilse Castan of mediated disputes over minor injuries, claimants who received an expression of sympathy were more willing to accept settlement offers than those who received none, even though the sympathy admitted no fault.

Nor need such laws work alone to be worthwhile. If people withhold apologies for many reasons, removing one of those reasons still helps; no one thinks a seatbelt law pointless because seatbelts do not prevent every traffic death.

Finally, the protection keeps out statements whose value as proof is small relative to the prejudice they create. Jurors tend to hear “I’m sorry” as “It was my fault,” though people routinely apologize for harms they did not cause. Excluding such statements makes verdicts more accurate, not less.

passages.title: Crab cues and periwinkle shells
passages.subject: natural-science
passages.text:
Along the coast of the Varn Peninsula, the banded periwinkle, a small grazing sea snail, differs strikingly between two neighboring bays. Periwinkles in Hesk Sound have shells nearly twice as thick as those of periwinkles in Tolley Inlet, only forty kilometers away. Because the snail’s larvae drift for weeks in coastal currents before settling, the two populations interbreed freely, and genetic surveys have found no differences between them. For years the contrast was attributed to the physical environment: Hesk Sound is more exposed to storm waves, and thicker shells were assumed to withstand being battered against rock.

The marine biologist Ruth Ambler doubted this account. Within Hesk Sound itself, she noted, periwinkles in sheltered coves have shells as thick as those on exposed headlands. What distinguishes the sound from the inlet, she observed, is not wave exposure but a predator: a shell-crushing crab that has been common in Hesk Sound for decades but has never become established in Tolley Inlet. Ambler proposed that shell thickness is not fixed at birth but is adjusted by each snail as it grows, in response to chemical cues that signal the presence of crabs.

To test this, Ambler collected newly settled juveniles from both bays and raised them in four sets of tanks. One set received seawater from tanks in which crabs were fed periwinkles; a second, water from tanks in which crabs were fed fish; a third, water containing crushed periwinkles but no crabs; and a fourth, plain seawater. After four months, snails in the first set had grown the thickest shells, those in the second and third sets shells of intermediate thickness, and those in the fourth the thinnest. Crucially, juveniles from Tolley Inlet and from Hesk Sound responded in the same way, so the difference between the wild populations could not reflect inherited differences between them. The experiment also suggests why the snails do not simply build thick shells everywhere. Those in the first set, though better armored, had added less body tissue than the snails raised in plain seawater. Shell material laid down on the inside of the shell takes up room the snail’s body would otherwise occupy, and building it diverts energy from growth. Where crabs are absent, a thin shell is the better bargain.

Ambler’s account has not settled every question. The concentrations of crab cues in her tanks were probably higher than those snails encounter in open water, and she has not ruled out that differences in the calcium content of the two bays’ water contribute to the pattern in the wild. Still, her experiment explains what the wave hypothesis could not: why sheltered and exposed snails in Hesk Sound are alike, and why genetically indistinguishable snails in the two bays are not.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Arne has shown that Strand built her phrases on the length of a dancer’s breath, and the company was therefore right to restore the original counts in its revivals.
The counts in Strand’s notebooks that fail to fit the music were long mistaken for errors, but they in fact reflect Strand’s indifference to the scores her dances were set to.
Arne convincingly explains the mismatched counts in Strand’s notebooks as a deliberate structural device, though his claim about the source of that device is less well supported.
Strand’s late works, in which the phrases never realign with the music, show that Arne’s account of how she organized her dances is mistaken.
Earlier revivals regularized Strand’s counts because their directors lacked the testimony of musicians who had worked with her, testimony that Arne has now supplied.
questions.explanation: The passage presents the puzzle of the mismatched counts (first paragraph), Arne’s convergence theory and its evidence (second and third), and then a reservation: the breath claim is thinly supported and the motive remains open (fourth). C captures both the endorsement and the reservation. A is the tempting trap, but it treats the breath claim as proven, which is exactly what the author doubts. D overstates the late works, which only suggest a change in Strand’s aims.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the one sentence the whole passage is built to support, including the author’s reservation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first sentence of the second paragraph (Arne’s claim) and the whole fourth paragraph (‘considerable advance’ … ‘Yet’ … ‘remains an open question’).

breakdown.analysis: So is the author on Arne’s side or not? Both. The third paragraph calls his evidence ‘persuasive,’ the fourth calls the theory ‘a considerable advance,’ and then the ‘Yet’ arrives: the breath part is thin, and why Strand built dances this way is still open. That’s the classic measured LSAT attitude: favorable with a reservation. We need an answer that says: Arne is right that the mismatches are deliberate structure, but his explanation of where they come from is weaker.

choices.note: Tempting. It sounds pro-Arne, and the company did restore the counts. But it says Arne ‘has shown’ the breath claim, and the fourth paragraph says that’s exactly the weak part. An answer that endorses the part the author doubts is wrong.
Wrong. Nobody says Strand was indifferent to the music. Arne says movement and music were designed to drift and then converge, which means she cared a lot about where they meet.

CORRECT. Endorsement (the mismatches are a deliberate device that organizes the dances) plus reservation (the breath explanation is less well supported). That’s the second through fourth paragraphs in one sentence.

Too strong. The late works suggest Strand’s aims changed late in her career; they don’t sink Arne’s account of the many dances where the convergence pattern holds. The author still says Arne ‘explains how many of Strand’s dances are built.’

We don’t know this. The passage never says why earlier directors regularized the counts beyond treating them as ‘slips of the pen,’ and the pianist’s memory is one piece of Arne’s evidence, not the point of the passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, earlier revivals of Strand’s dances
choices: restored the counts recorded in Strand’s notebooks wherever they conflicted with the music
relied on films of the original performances rather than on Strand’s notebooks
set Strand’s choreography to newly arranged scores written in four
moved the soloist’s entrance in Harbor Song to the beginning of a section of the score
altered the movement so that each phrase would begin on a downbeat
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the first paragraph says earlier revivals treated the mismatches as slips and regularized them, ‘stretching or compressing the movement so that each phrase began on a downbeat,’ which is E. A reverses the history: restoring the original counts is what the company did later, after Arne (fourth paragraph). B, C and D describe things the passage never mentions.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says the earlier revivals did.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last sentence of the first paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: This one is a straight lookup. The first paragraph: earlier revivals ‘treated such passages as slips of the pen and regularized them, stretching or compressing the movement so that each phrase began on a downbeat.’ We need an answer that says they changed the movement to fit the downbeat.

choices.note: Opposite. Restoring the original counts is what the company did after Arne’s work (first sentence of the fourth paragraph). The earlier revivals did the reverse.
Wrong. Films are never mentioned. The earlier directors worked from the notebooks; that’s how they knew the counts didn’t fit.
Wrong. The scores weren’t changed; the movement was. The music was already ‘in a steady four.’

We don’t know this. Nothing says the earlier revivals moved the soloist’s entrance. ‘Sections of the score’ comes from Arne’s finding in the third paragraph, not from a description of earlier revivals.
CORRECT. Nearly word for word from the first paragraph: they stretched or compressed the movement so each phrase began on a downbeat.

questions.stem: In the passage, the phrase “listen for the one” (near the end of the third paragraph) most probably refers to
choices: attending to the first beat of each measure as the cue for starting a phrase
matching each movement of a phrase to a separate note in the melody of the score
taking the timing of the whole ensemble from a single lead dancer or soloist
anticipating the beginning of each new section of the score so as to enter on time
counting each phrase from its first movement rather than from its last
questions.explanation: Strand told dancers not to ‘listen for the one’ but to count their own phrases and let ‘the music … find you’; what she rejected is the practice the earlier revivals imposed, beginning every phrase on a downbeat (first paragraph), which is A. D is tempting because the third paragraph mentions ‘the beginnings of sections of the score,’ but that phrase concerns where Arne found entrances do not fall, not what dancers listened for. E misreads ‘count their own phrases’ as a rule about where to start counting.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what Strand was telling dancers not to do when she forbade them to ‘listen for the one.’

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The pianist’s recollection, second-to-last sentence of the third paragraph, read against the last sentence of the first paragraph (phrases regularized to begin ‘on a downbeat’).

breakdown.analysis: Read the instruction as a contrast: don’t listen for the one; instead, count your own phrases and trust the music to find you. So ‘the one’ must be something in the music that dancers would normally use to time their phrases. The first paragraph tells us what that is: the earlier revivals made ‘each phrase began on a downbeat.’ The downbeat is the first beat of a measure, count ‘one.’ We need an answer that says: waiting for the music’s first beat to start a phrase.

choices.note: CORRECT. ‘The one’ is the downbeat, the first beat of a measure. Strand didn’t want dancers lining phrases up with it; she wanted them on their own count so the drift could happen. That’s exactly what the earlier revivals undid.
Wrong. Nothing in the passage is about melody notes. The issue is meter (counts and measures), not matching steps to tunes.
Wrong. The alternative Strand gave was ‘count their own phrases,’ which points away from following anyone else, dancer or musician. No lead dancer is mentioned.

Tempting. The third paragraph does mention ‘the beginnings of sections of the score.’ But that’s Arne’s finding about where entrances don’t fall, not Strand’s instruction to dancers. And ‘the one’ in a passage about counts and measures is a beat, not a section.
Wrong. This twists ‘count their own phrases’ into a rule about which end to count from. The contrast is between the dancer’s own count and the music’s count, not between ends of a phrase.

questions.stem: The author mentions the radio interview (third sentence of the fourth paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: provide evidence that Strand intended the phrases of her late works never to realign with the music
indicate that the main support for Arne’s claim about breath is open to another interpretation
show that Strand spoke more openly about her working methods late in her career than earlier
suggest that Strand regarded the dramatic content of her dances as more important than their structure
explain why rehearsal directors at first regarded the mismatched counts as errors
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the breath idea ‘derives from a single radio interview’ and that Strand’s remark ‘could as easily refer to dramatic need as to physiological need,’ so the interview is cited to show that the sole basis for the breath claim is ambiguous: B. D is the tempting trap because it picks up the word ‘dramatic,’ but the author only says the remark could refer to dramatic need, not that Strand ranked drama above structure. A attaches the interview to the late works, a separate point introduced by ‘Moreover.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the author brings up the radio interview.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second and third sentences of the fourth paragraph: ‘Yet the evidence for his claim about breath is much thinner…’ and the interview sentence after it.

breakdown.analysis: Why mention an interview at all? Look at the sentence just before it: the evidence for breath is ‘much thinner.’ Then the interview is offered as the only source for the breath idea, and the author says the quote could mean dramatic need just as easily as physical need. So the interview is the weak foundation, and the author is showing it can be read another way. Prephrase: to show that the breath claim rests on one ambiguous remark.

choices.note: Wrong job. The late works come up in the next sentence, after ‘Moreover,’ as a separate point. The interview is about breath, not about phrases that never realign.

CORRECT. The interview is the single source of the breath idea, and the author points out that the key remark fits a dramatic reading just as well. That’s showing the main support is open to another interpretation.
Wrong. We aren’t told when the interview happened, and nothing compares how openly she spoke early versus late. The point is the opposite: she said very little about method.

Tempting. It borrows ‘dramatic’ from the passage. But the author only says the remark ‘could as easily refer to dramatic need.’ Could is not did, and nothing says drama mattered more to her than structure. Too strong.
Wrong. The early directors’ view comes from the first paragraph and has nothing to do with the interview. The interview bears on Arne’s explanation, not on the earlier revivals.

questions.stem: Suppose a newly discovered notebook of Strand’s records an ensemble phrase of five counts that is performed several times in succession against music written throughout in three, with the first performance of the phrase beginning on a downbeat. If Arne’s account is correct, the notebook would be most likely to place a soloist’s entrance at the beginning of the
choices: third performance of the phrase
fifth performance of the phrase
fifth measure of the music
fourth performance of the phrase
seventh measure of the music
questions.explanation: On Arne’s account entrances fall where movement and music realign (third paragraph). Three phrases of five counts take fifteen counts, exactly five measures of three, so the fourth performance is the first since the opening to begin on a downbeat: D. B and E copy numbers from Harbor Song (the fifth phrase, seven measures), which worked only because that phrase was in seven against four; here the fifth performance starts on count 21 and the seventh measure on count 19, neither of which is a realignment point.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Apply Arne’s rule to a new case: where do phrase and music first line up again?

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: End of the second paragraph (the two cycles drift and converge) and the Harbor Song arithmetic in the second sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Don’t copy the Harbor Song answer. Rebuild the rule: an entrance comes when a new phrase starts on a downbeat, which happens when the counts used so far fill a whole number of measures. Phrases of 5 against measures of 3: 1. After 1 phrase: 5 counts (not a multiple of 3). 2. After 2: 10 (no). 3. After 3: 15 = 5 measures (yes). So the fourth performance starts on count 16, the downbeat of measure 6. That’s the first convergence, and Arne says entrances go there. Check: Harbor Song is the same logic, 4 × 7 = 28 = 7 × 4, so the fifth phrase.

choices.note: Wrong. The third performance starts on count 11. Ten counts used so far isn’t a multiple of 3, so it lands mid-measure.

Tempting. It’s the Harbor Song answer: there the fifth phrase was the entrance. But that came from 7 against 4. Here the fifth performance starts on count 21, after 20 counts, and 20 isn’t a multiple of 3. You can’t transfer the number, only the rule.
Wrong. Measure 5 starts on count 13. Twelve counts used isn’t a multiple of 5, so no phrase starts there; movement and music are still apart.

CORRECT. Three phrases of five = 15 counts = five measures of three, so the fourth performance is the first since the opening to begin on a downbeat. Arne says entrances fall at exactly these realignment points.
Tempting. ‘Seven measures’ is the Harbor Song number. Here measure 7 starts on count 19; 18 counts used isn’t a multiple of 5, so it’s the middle of a phrase.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about Arne’s account?
choices: It is undermined by the rehearsal pianist’s recollection, which suggests that Strand did not expect her dancers to keep count of their phrases at all.
It shows that the phrases in Strand’s late works were constructed on the same principle of convergence as those in Harbor Song.
It should not have led the company to restore the original counts in its revivals until Arne’s claim about breath had been confirmed.
It fails to explain why the entrances, exits, and lighting changes in many of Strand’s dances occur where they do.
It is better supported as an account of how many of Strand’s dances are organized than of why she organized them so.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the evidence for the breath claim is ‘much thinner’ than the evidence for the convergence pattern and ends: Arne ‘explains how many of Strand’s dances are built; why she built them that way remains an open question,’ which is E. C is the most tempting trap because the author does doubt the breath claim, but the restoration rests on the convergence pattern, which the author accepts. B contradicts the point about the late works, and D contradicts the third paragraph’s evidence.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement about Arne’s theory that matches the author’s precise mix of praise and doubt.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The whole fourth paragraph, especially its second and last sentences; the third paragraph for what the author calls ‘persuasive.’

breakdown.analysis: The author splits Arne’s theory in two. Part one, the convergence pattern (how the dances are built): strong, ‘persuasive,’ a ‘considerable advance.’ Part two, the breath claim (why she did it): thin, and ‘why she built them that way remains an open question.’ We need an answer that keeps that split: the how is well supported, the why is not.

choices.note: Opposite. The pianist’s recollection is part of Arne’s support: Strand told dancers to ‘count their own phrases.’ It fits the theory; it doesn’t undermine it.

Contradicts the fourth paragraph. In the late works the phrases ‘never realign with the music at all,’ which the author takes as a change in Strand’s aims. That’s not the Harbor Song principle of drifting toward convergence.

Tempting. The author does doubt the breath claim. But restoring the counts depends on the convergence pattern, which is the well-supported part; you don’t need to know why Strand drifted to know the counts weren’t slips. The author mentions the restoration approvingly, right next to ‘considerable advance.’
Opposite. Explaining where entrances, exits, and lighting changes fall is exactly what the theory does well (third paragraph: they fall ‘where movement and music realign’).

CORRECT. This is the last sentence of the fourth paragraph restated: Arne explains how many dances are built; why she built them that way is still open. The ‘many’ even matches the author’s hedge about the late works.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Halvey’s scrip failed to revive the town’s retail trade, because merchants returned most certificates to the treasury instead of spending them.
Kenning’s case that Halvey’s stamps caused its retail revival is undercut by an unclear notion of revival, a doubtful assumption, and a mishandled comparison.
Kenning’s study of Halvey shows that the design of a currency matters more to economic recovery than does the quantity of money in circulation.
The reopening of local employers, rather than the issuing of scrip, explains the recovery of retail sales in both Halvey and Corley.
Kenning’s reconstruction of the scrip’s circulation is ingenious, but the stamp records on which it depends cannot distinguish residents’ purchases from merchants’ tax payments.
questions.explanation: After presenting Kenning’s thesis, the author faults it in three steps: she does not clarify what the revival consists in (second paragraph), she assumes merchants passed scrip on (third), and she dismisses the Corley comparison too quickly (fourth), which ends by saying only that the stamps’ effect cannot be read from the sales figures. That is B. D is the most tempting trap, but the author says only that a reopened employer ‘could also have contributed’ and refuses to conclude that the stamps had no effect. A also overstates: the author never says the trade failed to revive.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the main point: the claim the whole passage supports.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: End of the first paragraph (Kenning’s thesis), the opening of the second (‘does not clarify’), the third (‘also assumes’), and the fourth (‘Finally’ … ‘None of this shows…’).

breakdown.analysis: This is the ‘scholar’s view, then what it fails to clarify, what it assumes, and what it can’t handle’ structure. The target is Kenning’s explanation of the revival, not the scrip itself and not the town. And the end of the fourth paragraph is careful: the stamps may have had some effect; you just can’t prove it from the sales figures. Prephrase: Kenning’s stamp explanation has three problems, so the sales figures don’t establish it.

choices.note: Too strong. The author never says trade didn’t revive; Corley’s and Halvey’s sales both ‘recovered.’ And the merchants’ tax payments are used to question Kenning’s mechanism, not to say the scrip failed.

CORRECT. Right target (Kenning’s claim about the stamps), and it lists all three criticisms: unclear ‘revival’ (second paragraph), the merchants assumption (third), and the brushed-off Corley comparison (fourth).
Wrong. The author credits Kenning for attending to design, but the whole passage argues her case isn’t proven. This turns a compliment into the thesis.

Tempting. The fourth paragraph does raise reopened employers. But the author says that ‘could also have contributed,’ then adds ‘None of this shows that the stamps were without effect.’ This claims a cause the author never commits to.
Wrong. The author calls the reconstruction ‘ingenious’ and never attacks the stamp records. The merchants’ tax payments come from ‘Kenning’s own figures,’ so the records are being used, not doubted.

questions.stem: According to the passage, most of Halvey’s scrip certificates
choices: were held by residents for several months before being spent at local shops
were tendered by council employees directly in payment of their property taxes
lost their validity because their holders had failed to affix the required weekly stamps
were returned to the town treasury by merchants in payment of property taxes
passed through the hands of several different merchants before finally reaching the treasury
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states that ‘most certificates returned to the town treasury within a few weeks, tendered by merchants in payment of property taxes,’ which is D. B is the tempting wrong-party trap: the employees received the scrip, but it was the merchants who paid it back in taxes. E contradicts the point of that paragraph, which is that merchants did not pass scrip on.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says happened to most certificates.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Lookup question, but watch who does what. The path in the third paragraph is: council employees → shopkeepers → treasury, and it’s the merchants who hand the certificates in, as property-tax payments, ‘within a few weeks.’ We need an answer with the merchants and the taxes.

choices.note: Opposite. The stamp charge pushed people to spend fast, and most certificates were back at the treasury ‘within a few weeks.’ Nothing says residents held them for months.
Tempting. Employees and property taxes are both in the passage. But the third paragraph says the certificates were ‘tendered by merchants.’ Right action, wrong party.
Wrong. The passage never says certificates went invalid for missing stamps, let alone most of them.
CORRECT. Third paragraph: ‘most certificates returned to the town treasury within a few weeks, tendered by merchants in payment of property taxes.’
Opposite. The author’s point is that merchants did not pass scrip on; it went from employees to shopkeepers and back to the treasury.

questions.stem: The passage provides information sufficient to answer which one of the following questions?
choices: How many certificates did Halvey’s council issue during the period in which the scrip circulated?
Why did Corley’s town council decide to issue its scrip without any stamp requirement?
Apart from goods sold by local merchants, what could Halvey’s scrip be used to pay for?
What proportion of Halvey’s retail sales during the scrip period were paid for in scrip?
How long after Halvey’s bank closed did one of the town’s mills resume partial operation?
questions.explanation: The first sentence of the passage says the certificates were ‘redeemable for town taxes,’ and the third paragraph confirms merchants used them to pay property taxes, so C can be answered: town taxes. E is the near-miss: the passage dates the mill’s partial reopening (summer of 1933) but says only that the bank was already closed in the autumn of 1932, never when it closed. A, B and D ask for figures or motives the passage never gives.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the one question the passage actually answers.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First sentence of the first paragraph (‘redeemable for town taxes’); also the second sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Can’t prephrase the question, so test each one against the text. For each, ask: could I point to the sentence that answers it? Only one survives. Watch for questions that use passage words (bank, mill, Corley) but need a fact the passage doesn’t supply.

choices.note: We don’t know. The passage mentions ‘most certificates’ but never gives a number issued.
We don’t know. The passage says Corley issued scrip ‘without any stamp requirement’ but never says why its council made that choice.
CORRECT. The certificates were ‘redeemable for town taxes,’ and merchants used them ‘in payment of property taxes.’ So the answer is: town taxes.
We don’t know. The passage talks about sales and about scrip, but never says what share of sales scrip paid for.

Tempting. The mill date is given (summer of 1933), and the bank is mentioned. But the passage says only that the bank was already closed in the autumn of 1932; it never says when it closed. Half the answer is missing.

questions.stem: The primary function of the third paragraph is to
choices: identify an assumption on which Kenning’s argument relies and cite evidence from her own work that tells against it
show that the stamp records on which Kenning bases her reconstruction of the scrip’s circulation are unreliable and incomplete
clarify an ambiguity in Kenning’s use of the term “revival” that the preceding paragraph left unresolved
explain why Halvey’s council chose to make its scrip redeemable for town taxes rather than for goods or cash
present a comparison between Halvey and another town that Kenning had dismissed too quickly in her study
questions.explanation: The third paragraph opens ‘Her argument also assumes that merchants passed scrip on as readily as residents did’ and then notes that ‘Kenning’s own figures suggest otherwise,’ which is A. B is tempting because the paragraph draws on her figures, but it uses them rather than doubting them; the second paragraph even calls the reconstruction ingenious. C describes the second paragraph’s job and E the fourth’s.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe what the third paragraph does in the author’s argument.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First two sentences of the third paragraph; compare the jobs of the second and fourth paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: Read the opening words: ‘Her argument also assumes…’ So this paragraph is the assumption criticism. Then: ‘Kenning’s own figures suggest otherwise.’ The evidence against the assumption comes from her own data. The rest of the paragraph spells out what the scrip may really have been doing. Prephrase: name an assumption Kenning makes and use her own numbers against it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Both halves check out: the assumption (merchants passed scrip on as readily as residents) and the counterevidence from ‘Kenning’s own figures.’

Tempting. The paragraph does lean on her figures. But it relies on them; it doesn’t say they’re unreliable. The second paragraph calls the reconstruction ‘ingenious.’ The problem is her inference, not her records.
Wrong paragraph. The ‘revival’ ambiguity is the second paragraph’s criticism, and the third never returns to it.
Wrong. The paragraph says what tax redemption let the scrip do in effect, but never explains why the council chose that design, and nothing is said about goods or cash as alternatives.
Wrong paragraph. The Corley comparison is the fourth paragraph.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the second paragraph?
choices: Kenning’s figures show that the total value of Halvey’s retail sales stagnated while the scrip circulated.
A charge that makes holding money costly could increase the number of purchases without increasing the total spent.
Halvey’s merchants recorded the number of their transactions more accurately than the value of their sales.
Residents of Halvey generally preferred to make several small purchases rather than a single large one of equal value.
Kenning should have measured Halvey’s revival by the number of transactions rather than by the value of sales.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the number of transactions ‘could rise sharply even while total sales stagnated, if residents merely broke their purchases into smaller ones in order to pass on scrip before the next stamp came due,’ which is B stated generally. A is the tempting trap: it turns the author’s ‘could’ into a finding from Kenning’s figures. E takes a side the author never takes; the complaint is that Kenning wavers between the measures, not that she chose the wrong one.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the second paragraph supports, without going beyond it.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Last two sentences of the second paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase exactly, but the paragraph makes one real claim: counting transactions and counting dollars can come apart. The stamp makes holding scrip costly, so people may split purchases to pass it on before the stamp is due. More transactions, same total spending. Watch for answers that turn ‘could’ into ‘did’ or pick a side on which measure is right.

choices.note: Tempting. It uses the paragraph’s own words, but the author says total sales ‘could’ stagnate while transactions rise. It never says Kenning’s figures show stagnation. A possibility isn’t a finding.
CORRECT. This is the second paragraph’s mechanism in general form: the stamp makes holding scrip costly, people split purchases, transactions go up, total spending may not.
We don’t know this. The paragraph says Kenning switches between the two measures, not that one was recorded more accurately.
Wrong. Residents might split purchases to avoid the stamp, which is not a preference for small purchases. And the paragraph says this only could happen.

Too far. The author’s complaint is that Kenning doesn’t clarify which she means. If anything, the paragraph suggests transaction counts are the weaker measure, since they can rise without more spending.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward Kenning’s study is most accurately described as
choices: dismissive rejection of both its methods and its conclusions as fundamentally misguided
agreement with its conclusions combined with doubts about the reliability of its sources
admiration for aspects of its method combined with skepticism about its central causal claim
general approval tempered by a concern that it overstates the importance of taxation
reluctant acceptance of its conclusion owing to the absence of any better explanation
questions.explanation: The second paragraph praises Kenning for attending to a currency’s design and calls her reconstruction ‘ingenious’; the rest of the passage argues that her causal claim about the stamps is not established. That is C. D is the near-miss: the author does have a reservation, but it runs the other way, since the author thinks taxation explains more than Kenning allows. A ignores the praise, and B and E credit the author with accepting a conclusion the author doubts.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pin down the author’s mix of praise and criticism of Kenning.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: First sentence of the second paragraph (the praise), then the criticisms in the second through fourth paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: Is the author for or against Kenning? Both, about different things. Method: ‘has the merit of attending to the design,’ reconstruction ‘ingenious.’ Conclusion: unclear, resting on a doubtful assumption, and ignoring a comparison case. We need: likes the method, doubts the causal claim. Attitude answers are moderated; reject anything that overshoots in either direction.

choices.note: Too strong. The author praises Kenning’s attention to design and her ‘ingenious’ reconstruction, and even says the stamps may have had some effect. This isn’t wholesale rejection.
Backwards. The author doubts Kenning’s conclusion and uses her sources (‘Kenning’s own figures’) without questioning them.
CORRECT. Admiration for parts of the method (design focus, ingenious reconstruction) plus skepticism about the claim that the stamps explain the revival. That’s the passage’s shape.

Tempting. ‘Approval tempered by a concern’ sounds like a measured LSAT attitude. But the concern is reversed: the author suggests taxation did more than Kenning credits (‘what a cash-starved municipality can accomplish with its power to tax’). Kenning never stresses taxation at all.
Wrong. The author doesn’t accept Kenning’s conclusion, reluctantly or otherwise. The point is that the evidence doesn’t establish it.

questions.stem: With which one of the following statements would the author be most likely to agree?
choices: The revival of Halvey’s retail trade was produced chiefly by the partial reopening of one of the town’s mills.
Kenning erred in relying on the surviving stamp records to reconstruct how Halvey’s scrip circulated among the town’s residents.
Tax-redeemable scrip without a stamp requirement might have served Halvey’s council equally well as a way to pay its employees.
The experience of Corley demonstrates that the stamps had no effect on how quickly Halvey’s scrip was spent by its residents.
Historians of scrip should attend to the quantity of money issued rather than to the design of the currency.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the scrip may have functioned as a way for the town to pay employees out of future tax receipts, ‘a useful arrangement, but not one that the stamps were needed to produce’; Corley’s stamp-free scrip and the closing emphasis on the town’s ‘power to tax’ point the same way, so C. A and D are the tempting traps: the author says a reopened mill ‘could also have contributed’ and explicitly denies having shown that the stamps had no effect. B contradicts the praise of the reconstruction as ‘ingenious,’ and E reverses the credit given to Kenning for attending to design.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the statement the author would accept, given the exact strength of the author’s claims.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: End of the third paragraph (‘not one that the stamps were needed to produce’), the last two sentences of the fourth paragraph, and the compliments at the start of the second.

breakdown.analysis: The author is careful. Notice what the author does and doesn’t commit to: 1. The stamps may have done something (‘None of this shows…’). 2. The mill ‘could’ have contributed, not ‘did.’ 3. The tax-receipt arrangement was useful and didn’t need the stamps (third paragraph). So the safe answer is one built on point 3, hedged like the author. Prephrase: the town could have paid its workers with tax-redeemable scrip even without stamps.

choices.note: Tempting. The mill is the author’s best counterpoint to Kenning. But the author only says it ‘could also have contributed.’ ‘Chiefly produced’ is a commitment the author never makes. Too strong.
Opposite. The author calls the reconstruction ‘ingenious’ and uses Kenning’s own figures in the third paragraph. The records aren’t the problem.

CORRECT. Third paragraph: paying employees out of future tax receipts was ‘a useful arrangement, but not one that the stamps were needed to produce.’ A stamp-free, tax-redeemable scrip would give you that arrangement, and the hedge ‘might have’ matches the author’s caution.

Tempting. Corley is the author’s comparison case. But the fourth paragraph says flat out, ‘None of this shows that the stamps were without effect.’ This puts in the author’s mouth exactly what the author disclaims.
Opposite. The second paragraph credits Kenning for ‘attending to the design of a currency rather than merely to its quantity.’ The author likes that move.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help Kenning to answer the objection concerning Corley that is raised in the fourth paragraph?
choices: Corley’s scrip, like Halvey’s, could be used to pay property taxes owed to the town, and merchants there often used it that way.
Corley’s merchants’ association recorded the total value of its members’ sales but not the number of their transactions.
Fewer of Corley’s merchants than of Halvey’s agreed to accept the scrip issued by their town during its first year.
Some other towns in the region that issued scrip with a stamp requirement saw no recovery in retail sales.
Halvey’s retail sales had risen nearly as far by the spring of 1933 as they would rise while the scrip circulated.
questions.explanation: The objection is that Kenning cannot dismiss Corley because of its reopened railway shop when Halvey also had a reopened employer, a mill that resumed partial operation in the summer of 1933. E shows that nearly all of Halvey’s recovery came before that reopening, so the mill cannot explain it and the two towns are no longer parallel. B is tempting because it recalls the second paragraph’s transactions-versus-value point, but it does nothing about the alternative cause. A and C make Corley a cleaner case against the stamps, and D weakens Kenning.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that best rescues Kenning from the Corley objection.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The fourth paragraph through its fourth sentence, especially Halvey’s mill ‘resumed partial operation in the summer of 1933’; the timing in the first paragraph (scrip from the autumn of 1932, for eighteen months).

breakdown.analysis: Lay out the objection. 1. Corley had no stamps and recovered just as fast. 2. Kenning says Corley’s recovery came from its reopened railway shop. 3. Author: fine, but Halvey had a reopened mill too, so maybe that explains Halvey’s recovery. So the objection lives on the Halvey mill. How does Kenning escape? Cut the mill off from Halvey’s recovery. If the recovery mostly happened before the mill reopened, the mill can’t be the cause, and Halvey is no longer like Corley. Prephrase: Halvey recovered before the mill came back. The right answer gives you that only through a date, so you have to connect ‘spring of 1933’ with ‘summer of 1933.’

choices.note: Wrong direction. If Corley’s scrip also redeemed for taxes and was used that way, the two towns share the tax mechanism from the third paragraph and differ mainly in the stamps. That makes Corley look like a fair test showing stamps weren’t needed, which hurts Kenning.

Tempting. It sounds like the second paragraph’s point about transactions versus total value, and it suggests Corley’s figures measure value. But the objection is about an alternative cause (a reopened employer), and this does nothing about Halvey’s mill.

Wrong direction. If fewer Corley merchants took scrip yet Corley recovered just as fast, scrip (stamped or not) looks less important to recovery. That doesn’t help a stamps-explain-the-revival thesis.
Wrong direction. Stamped scrip with no recovery elsewhere is a point against Kenning, not a defense of her.

CORRECT. The mill resumed operation in the summer of 1933. If nearly all of Halvey’s rise had happened by spring, the mill can’t account for it, and the author’s ‘Halvey had a reopened employer too’ reply loses its force. Kenning’s distinction between the towns stands.

questions.stem: According to passage A, the physicians whom Brann asked about medical errors
choices: apologized less often after medical errors than other hospital staff did
said they would apologize more readily if apology statutes were adopted
cited legal exposure more often than any other reason for not apologizing
gave reasons other than legal exposure for not apologizing
reported that institutional habit discouraged their patients from suing the hospital
questions.explanation: The third paragraph of passage A says the physicians cited embarrassment, uncertainty, and institutional habit ‘at least as often as legal exposure,’ so they gave reasons other than legal exposure, D. C is the trap: ‘at least as often’ means legal exposure was not cited more often than the others. A, B, and E mention things the passage never states.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A actually says about Brann’s interviews.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph (second sentence).

breakdown.analysis: Go back and read the sentence. Physicians “cited embarrassment, uncertainty about what had gone wrong, and institutional habit at least as often as legal exposure.” So legal exposure was one reason, and there were others that came up just as much. We want the choice that says that, nothing more.

choices.note: Brann asked physicians only. No comparison to other staff appears anywhere.
Nothing about what they’d do under a statute. If anything, passage A uses Brann to suggest the statutes won’t change much.
Reverses the finding. “At least as often as legal exposure” means legal exposure did not come out on top.
CORRECT. Embarrassment, uncertainty, and habit are all reasons other than legal exposure, and the passage says the physicians cited them.
Institutional habit was a reason physicians didn’t apologize. It has nothing to do with patients deciding not to sue. Right words, wrong relationship.

questions.stem: In saying that ‘sincerity is not measured by legal risk’ (second sentence of passage B), the author of passage B most probably means that
choices: apologies that carry no legal risk are usually more sincere than those that could be used in court
an apology’s sincerity is independent of whether it could later be used as evidence against the apologizer
courts are not in a position to determine whether an apology offered after an accident is sincere
people who apologize at the scene of an accident rarely consider the legal consequences of doing so
an apology that carries legal risk is less likely to be offered than one that does not
questions.explanation: The phrase answers critics who suppose regret can be sincere ‘only when it is costly’; B’s author replies that a protected apology can be fully meant, as with the driver who ‘may mean it entirely, whether or not the words could later be read to a jury.’ That is B. A overcorrects by making protected apologies more sincere, and E states the statutes’ rationale, which is true in spirit but not what this phrase means.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Translate the phrase in context.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first paragraph: the critics’ view in the first sentence and the driver example in the third.

breakdown.analysis: Read the sentence before: critics act “as if regret could be sincere only when it is costly.” The phrase is the reply. Then the driver example: he “may mean it entirely,” jury or no jury. So: legal risk and sincerity are unrelated. Risk doesn’t make an apology sincere, and the lack of risk doesn’t make it fake. We want “sincerity doesn’t depend on legal risk.”

choices.note: Too strong. Passage B says sincerity doesn’t depend on risk, not that low-risk apologies are more sincere. That just flips the critics’ error.
CORRECT. Heartfelt or not is a separate question from whether the words could be used in court. That’s exactly what the driver example shows.
Courts and their abilities never come up here. The point is about apologies, not judges.
Passage B says the driver may be sincere “whether or not” the words could be used. It doesn’t claim people don’t think about consequences.
Tempting, because this is the idea behind apology laws. But this phrase is about sincerity, not about how often people apologize.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately characterizes the relationship between the two passages?
choices: Passage A describes the origins of a type of law; passage B evaluates the empirical evidence for that law’s effectiveness.
Passage A defends a type of law against several criticisms; passage B argues that the law should be broadened considerably.
Passage A raises objections to a type of law; passage B defends that type of law, implicitly answering some of those objections.
Passage A argues that a type of law has failed to achieve its goals; passage B argues that those goals were mistaken.
Passage A and passage B offer competing accounts of why people who have caused an injury are reluctant to apologize.
questions.explanation: Passage A lists three problems with apology statutes (‘First… Second… Third…’), and passage B defends such laws, answering A’s worries about unsatisfying sympathy and about the many reasons people withhold apologies without naming A. That is C. D is the tempting trap: A does doubt the laws work, but B never calls the laws’ goals mistaken; it says the laws serve those goals. A, B, and E misdescribe one or both passages.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Label each passage, then find the choice that matches both labels.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The first paragraph of each passage, plus passage A’s ‘First… Second… Third…’ paragraphs and passage B’s second and third paragraphs.

breakdown.analysis: What is each passage doing? A: “they rest on uncertain ground,” then three numbered problems. That’s a critique. B: “Critics… sometimes treat…”, then “It is true that… But…”, “Nor need such laws…”, “Finally…”. That’s a defense, and several of its points line up with A’s problems without naming A. We need: A objects, B defends.

choices.note: A doesn’t tell the history of the statutes; it attacks them. And B isn’t a neutral evaluation of evidence. It argues for the laws.
Backwards on A. A is the critic, not the defender. And B never asks for broader laws.

CORRECT. A gives three objections; B defends apology laws and answers at least two of A’s worries (unsatisfying sympathy, many reasons for not apologizing). It never answers A’s third point, which is why “some of those objections” is exactly right.

Tempting on the first half: A does think the statutes may not deliver. But B doesn’t say the goals were wrong. B says the laws help achieve them (more apologies, more settlements, more accurate verdicts).

Only one paragraph of A (the third) is about why people don’t apologize, and B doesn’t offer a competing account of that; it grants there are ‘many reasons.’ Too narrow a description of both passages.

questions.stem: The author of passage B mentions a seatbelt law (third paragraph of passage B) primarily in order to
choices: suggest that apology statutes, like seatbelt laws, will eventually be adopted in nearly every jurisdiction in the country
show that laws intended to change people’s behavior are seldom as effective as their supporters claim
provide evidence that fear of legal consequences is the main reason that people fail to apologize after accidents
illustrate the difficulty of measuring a law’s effects when the problem it targets has many causes
support the view that a law can be worthwhile even if it removes only one cause of a problem
questions.explanation: The seatbelt example backs the sentence before it: if people withhold apologies for many reasons, removing one still helps. Seatbelts don’t prevent every death, yet no one calls the law pointless, which is E. B is the trap; the example concedes that laws are not complete solutions, but its point is that partial help is still worth having, not that such laws generally disappoint. C contradicts B’s concession that there are many reasons.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say why the seatbelt example is there.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, third paragraph, read against passage A’s third paragraph (the many reasons physicians don’t apologize).

breakdown.analysis: Why mention seatbelts in a passage about apologies? It’s an analogy. The claim right before it: “If people withhold apologies for many reasons, removing one of those reasons still helps.” Seatbelts don’t stop every death, but the law isn’t pointless. Same for apology laws: they remove only one obstacle (fear of being sued), but that’s still worth something. This answers A’s second objection, that “a rule of evidence can do nothing” about the other reasons.

choices.note: Nothing about adoption trends. The example is about whether partial help is worthwhile.
Tempting, because the example admits seatbelts don’t prevent every death. But the point is the opposite of “laws seldom work”: it’s that a partly effective law is still worthwhile.
B grants that there are “many reasons.” The example doesn’t make legal fear the main one.
Measurement isn’t the issue. The example takes for granted that seatbelts help; it borrows ‘many causes’ from the passage but not its point.
CORRECT. One cause removed, problem not fully solved, measure still worth having. That’s the seatbelt point, applied to apology laws.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the use of apology statutes that the author of passage A calls ‘most troubling’ (first sentence of the last paragraph of passage A)?
choices: A retailer trains staff to give scripted expressions of concern, which a consumer law makes inadmissible, so that customers with valid complaints will drop them.
A hospital encourages its physicians to admit their errors openly, even though doing so increases the hospital’s exposure to costly malpractice lawsuits.
A city protects bystanders from liability when they give aid at accident scenes, and as a result more bystanders begin to offer aid.
A landlord refuses to apologize to tenants for a flood in their building because he fears that an apology would be used against him in court.
A driver apologizes after a collision and later learns, to his relief, that a statute prevents the apology from being introduced as evidence against him.
questions.explanation: The ‘most troubling’ use is an insurer coaching policyholders to give legally weightless regret in order to defuse claims that deserve to be pursued: a protection meant for genuine apology is exploited to make valid claims go away. A matches every element. D is the trap, since it is also about apologies and lawsuits, but it describes the reluctance the statutes were meant to cure, not their exploitation; C and E show the law working as intended, and B involves no protection at all.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Match the structure of passage A’s third objection in a new setting.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, last paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Break the scenario into parts: 1. a legal protection meant to encourage genuine apology; 2. someone with an interest in limiting payouts coaches people to use it; 3. the apologies are carefully emptied of legal weight; 4. the goal is to make deserving claims disappear. We want a case with all four, especially the cynical use and the valid claims.

choices.note: CORRECT. Protected, scripted concern (1–3), used so that customers with valid complaints back off (4). That’s the insurer’s move in a store.
The opposite: real admissions despite legal risk. No protection is being gamed.
This is the protection doing what it’s supposed to do. Nothing strategic or cynical.
Tempting because it’s about apologies and lawsuits. But this is the original problem the statutes address (fear of liability), not their misuse.
A sincere apology that happens to be protected. No coaching, no aim of defeating a valid claim.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over whether
choices: a sympathetic apology that admits no fault offers many injured people something of real value
fear of litigation is one of the reasons that people withhold apologies after causing harm
some injured people want an admission of fault and not merely an expression of sympathy from the other party
most apology statutes protect expressions of sympathy but leave admissions of fault fully admissible
jurors tend to interpret a defendant’s expression of sympathy as an admission of fault
questions.explanation: Passage A says a sympathy-only apology is the kind injured people find ‘least satisfying’ and ‘gives injured people little of what they actually seek,’ while passage B says that for many injured people ‘what matters first is acknowledgment of the harm done’ and backs it with Castan’s settlement finding. That is a direct disagreement, A. B and C are points both authors accept, D is stated by A and not contested by B, and E is the trap: B asserts it, but A says nothing about how jurors hear apologies.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find a claim one author would affirm and the other would deny.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A’s second paragraph (sympathy-only apologies give injured people little of what they seek) against passage B’s second paragraph (acknowledgment matters first; Castan’s study).

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one author must say yes and the other no. Silence on one side doesn’t count. So for each choice, check both passages. The clash is the value of sympathy-only apologies to the injured. A: they’re the “least satisfying” kind and give injured people “little of what they actually seek.” B: for many, “what matters first is acknowledgment,” and claimants who got sympathy with no admission were more willing to settle. Note A’s third objection doesn’t change this: A thinks weightless regret can be used to make claims go away, not that it gives the injured anything of real value.

choices.note: CORRECT. A says a sympathy-only apology gives injured people little of what they seek; B says acknowledgment is what many of them want first. Yes versus no on the same question.
Both agree. A says physicians cited other reasons “at least as often as legal exposure,” so legal exposure is one reason. B says removing “one of those reasons still helps.”
Both agree. A says the statutes promote the apology people “find least satisfying,” and B concedes “some injured people want the latter.”
A states this outright, and B never contests it (“a protected statement of sympathy is not a confession of fault”). No disagreement.
Tempting, since this is B’s argument and A is the critic. But A never discusses jurors or how they hear apologies. You can’t disagree with a point you never address.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a criticism that the author of passage A would be most likely to offer regarding the study by Castan described in passage B?
choices: Claimants in mediated disputes over minor injuries are unlike most injured people, since most injured people never enter mediation at all.
Expressions of sympathy that carry no admission of fault are rarely sincere, so the claimants in the study were misled.
Claimants may have been more willing to settle only because they feared that the expressions of sympathy would be used against them.
Claimants’ greater willingness to settle does not show that the claims they gave up were ones they ought to have given up.
The study shows only that apology statutes increase the number of apologies offered, not that they reduce the number of lawsuits.
questions.explanation: Passage B presents Castan’s finding (sympathy made claimants more willing to settle) as a point in favor of apology laws. Passage A’s third objection is that weightless expressions of regret may ‘defuse claims that deserve to be pursued,’ so A’s author would say that easier settlement is not a good result in itself, which is D. A is the strongest trap, a generic sampling complaint that nothing in passage A supports. B is the view passage B attributes to critics, but A’s author never questions anyone’s sincerity; C is incoherent, and E misdescribes the study.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the objection passage A’s author would raise to passage B’s use of the Castan study.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, second paragraph (Castan) against passage A’s last paragraph (strategic use).

breakdown.analysis: Passage B treats “more willing to accept settlement offers” as good news. Ask: good for whom? A’s third problem says an insurer can use weightless regret to “defuse claims that deserve to be pursued.” From A’s side, Castan’s result could be exactly that problem in action. People settled, but maybe they shouldn’t have. It’s like a store showing that customers stop complaining after a friendly apology. That proves the apology works on customers, not that their complaints were wrong. The answer must come from A’s own concerns, not just any criticism you could think of.

choices.note: The big trap. It sounds like a sharp methodological point. But A never mentions mediation or who ends up in it. This criticism comes from you, not from A’s author.

Tempting, because B says critics treat these apologies as insincere. But that’s B’s characterization. A’s author never questions sincerity; A’s first problem is that such apologies are unsatisfying, not fake.
Makes no sense. The sympathy in the study admitted no fault, and fear of its use would push people away from settling, not toward it.
CORRECT. This is A’s third objection aimed at B’s evidence: settlement may just mean a deserving claim was defused, which is what A fears these laws make possible.
Misdescribes the study. Castan measured willingness to settle, not how many apologies were offered under a statute.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: Periwinkles in Hesk Sound have thicker shells than those in Tolley Inlet chiefly because Hesk Sound is more exposed to storm waves.

Although they are genetically indistinguishable, the periwinkles of Hesk Sound and Tolley Inlet have evolved different shell thicknesses in response to the presence or absence of a shell-crushing crab.
Ambler’s experiment shows that building a thick shell slows a periwinkle’s growth, which explains why most periwinkles have thin shells.
The thickness of a periwinkle’s shell depends mainly on the calcium content of the water in which it grows, not on predators.
Experimental evidence supports Ambler’s view that the two bays’ shell difference reflects each snail’s response to chemical cues from crabs, though questions remain.
questions.explanation: The passage presents Ambler’s hypothesis that snails thicken their shells in response to crab cues, describes the experiment supporting it, and ends by noting open questions while affirming that it explains what the wave hypothesis could not. That is E. B is the trap: ‘evolved’ implies inherited differences, which the experiment rules out. A is the view Ambler rejects, C is a detail from the second half of the third paragraph, and D is only a possibility the author raises.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the sentence that sums up the whole passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: The last sentence of the second paragraph (Ambler’s proposal) and the fourth paragraph (the verdict).

breakdown.analysis: Puzzle: same genes, different shells. Old answer: waves. Ambler: no, it’s crab cues, and each snail adjusts its own shell. Experiment backs her. Last paragraph: some questions left, ‘still’ her account explains what the wave idea couldn’t. The main point should have Ambler’s idea, the support for it, and a slight hedge.

choices.note: That’s the old view, the one Ambler rejects with the sheltered-cove evidence.
Tempting. But “evolved” is the problem. Evolution means inherited differences. The experiment shows juveniles from both bays responded the same way, so the difference is not inherited.
One detail from the third paragraph, and it overstates: the passage never says most periwinkles have thin shells.
The author mentions calcium only as something Ambler hasn’t ruled out. Not the main point, and not supported as the main cause.
CORRECT. Ambler’s cue hypothesis, supported by the experiment, with the author’s noted reservations. That covers the whole passage.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following led Ambler to doubt that exposure to storm waves explains the thickness of Hesk Sound periwinkles’ shells?
choices: Genetic surveys revealed no differences between the periwinkles of the two bays despite their differing shells.
Snails in sheltered coves of Hesk Sound have shells as thick as those on its exposed headlands.
Tolley Inlet is at least as exposed to storm waves as Hesk Sound is, though its snails are thinner-shelled.
Thick-shelled periwinkles add less body tissue as they grow than thin-shelled periwinkles do.
A shell-crushing crab common in Hesk Sound has never become established in Tolley Inlet.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says Ambler doubted the wave account and immediately gives her reason: within Hesk Sound, snails in sheltered coves have shells as thick as those on exposed headlands, which is B. E is the trap; the crab’s absence from Tolley Inlet is part of her alternative explanation, not her reason for rejecting the wave account. A is background, C contradicts the first paragraph, and D comes from the later experiment.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the specific observation that made Ambler doubt the wave explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Second paragraph, first two sentences.

breakdown.analysis: “Ambler doubted this account. Within Hesk Sound itself, she noted…” The very next sentence is the reason. If waves made shells thick, sheltered snails should have thinner shells than exposed ones. They don’t. That’s the evidence against waves.

choices.note: Background from the first paragraph. Genetic sameness doesn’t, by itself, count against waves, and the passage doesn’t present it as Ambler’s reason.
CORRECT. Same thickness in sheltered and exposed spots means wave exposure isn’t what’s driving thickness.
Contradicts the passage: Hesk Sound is “more exposed to storm waves.”
This is a later experimental result about the cost of thick shells (third paragraph). It didn’t lead her to doubt the wave idea.
Tempting, since it’s part of her reasoning. But it supports her crab hypothesis; the stem asks what made her doubt the wave hypothesis.

questions.stem: The author mentions that the snails in the first set of tanks had added less body tissue than those raised in plain seawater (sixth sentence of the third paragraph) primarily in order to
choices: help explain why periwinkles do not build thick shells in places where crabs are absent
provide evidence that the snails in the first set of tanks were exposed to the most concentrated cues
identify a limitation of the experiment to which the author returns in the final paragraph
show that thick shells protect periwinkles from crabs less well than earlier researchers had believed
suggest that a snail’s growth, rather than its shell, is what protects it from being eaten by crabs
questions.explanation: The sentence before it announces that the experiment ‘also suggests why the snails do not simply build thick shells everywhere’; the body-tissue finding shows that thickening costs growth, so where crabs are absent ‘a thin shell is the better bargain.’ That is A. E is the trap: growth is what a thin shell buys, but the passage never says growth protects the snail. C misplaces the limitations, which come only in the fourth paragraph, and B and D invent claims about cue strength and shell protection.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Say what job the body-tissue finding does.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, fifth through eighth sentences (‘The experiment also suggests…’ through ‘…the better bargain’).

breakdown.analysis: Why bring up body tissue in a passage about shells? Read the sentence before it: the experiment ‘also suggests why the snails do not simply build thick shells everywhere.’ So the finding answers a natural question: if thick shells protect, why not always build them? Answer: they cost growth. The next two sentences spell out the cost, and the last one draws the verdict for crab-free water. Prephrase: to explain why thick shells aren’t built where there are no crabs.

choices.note: CORRECT. The finding shows the cost of thickening (less body tissue), which is why, without crabs, a thin shell is ‘the better bargain.’
Wrong. Nothing ties body tissue to cue concentration. And the concentration worry in the fourth paragraph is about tanks versus open water, not about which tank set got the strongest cue.
Tempting, since the fourth paragraph does list limitations. But the body-tissue finding isn’t one of them, and the author never returns to it there. It’s a result, not a flaw.
Wrong. The finding is about cost, not protection. The passage still says the first-set snails were ‘better armored.’
Tempting: faster growth is what thin shells buy. But the passage never says growth protects a snail from crabs. The trade is growth versus armor you don’t need.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?
choices: The cues from crabs fed periwinkles produced the thickest shells because they were the most concentrated cues used in the experiment.
Adult periwinkles moved from Hesk Sound to Tolley Inlet would soon develop shells as thin as those of Tolley Inlet periwinkles.
Periwinkles raised in water containing crushed periwinkles grew thinner shells than those raised in water from tanks of crabs fed fish.
Cues from crabs alone are sufficient to produce shells as thick as those of wild periwinkles in Hesk Sound.
Periwinkles can respond to cues from crushed members of their own species even when no crab is present.
questions.explanation: In the third tank set, water held crushed periwinkles but no crabs, and those snails grew shells of intermediate thickness, thicker than the plain-seawater controls. So periwinkles respond to cues from crushed periwinkles even without crab cues, which is E. C is the trap: the passage puts the second and third sets together at ‘intermediate thickness’ and gives no ranking between them. A invents a cause, B assumes shells can thin, and D compares tank snails to wild ones, which the passage never does.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the claim the experiment’s results actually support.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Third paragraph, second and third sentences: the four tank sets and their results.

breakdown.analysis: Hard to prephrase, so lay out the results. 1. Crabs fed periwinkles → thickest. 2. Crabs fed fish → intermediate. 3. Crushed periwinkles, no crabs → intermediate. 4. Plain seawater → thinnest. Set 3 has no crab at all, yet beats plain seawater. So the snails react to crushed periwinkles on their own. Watch for answers that rank sets 2 and 3 or explain why set 1 won; the passage gives neither.

choices.note: Invents a cause. The passage never says set 1 had more concentrated cues. The simpler reading is that it combined crab cues with cues from eaten periwinkles.
We don’t know this. The passage never says shells can thin, and adults in particular have already laid down their shell material.
Tempting, since you might expect crab cues to matter more. But the passage lumps sets 2 and 3 together as “intermediate thickness.” No ranking between them is given.
No comparison between tank shells and wild Hesk Sound shells is made, so “sufficient to match the wild” is unsupported.
CORRECT. Set 3 had crushed periwinkles but no crabs, and its snails still grew thicker shells than the plain-seawater set.

questions.stem: Which one of the following experiments would be most useful in determining whether the difference in calcium content mentioned in the second sentence of the fourth paragraph contributes to the difference in shell thickness between the two bays’ periwinkles?
choices: raising juveniles from both bays in plain seawater and comparing the thickness of the shells that the two groups develop
raising juveniles in water from tanks of crabs fed periwinkles at several different concentrations of crab cue and then comparing the thickness of their shells
comparing the shell thickness of periwinkles living in sheltered parts of Tolley Inlet with that of periwinkles in its exposed parts
raising juveniles without crab cues in water matched to Hesk Sound’s calcium level and in water matched to Tolley Inlet’s, then comparing shells
measuring the calcium content of shells collected from each of the two bays and comparing the averages for the two populations
questions.explanation: To learn whether calcium matters, vary calcium while holding everything else, including crab cues, constant; D does exactly that with the two bays’ calcium levels. B is the trap, because it tests the other reservation in the same sentence, cue concentration, not calcium. A repeats the test for inherited differences, C tests waves, and E measures shell composition without showing what causes thickness.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Pick the experiment that isolates calcium as a cause of thickness.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, second sentence (the calcium reservation), using the third paragraph’s tank experiment as a model.

breakdown.analysis: To test one factor, change only that factor. Here: two calcium levels (Hesk’s and Tolley’s), same kind of snails, no crab cues to muddy things, then compare shells. If the Hesk-level calcium gives thicker shells, calcium contributes. If not, it doesn’t. Anything that varies something else, or just measures shells, can’t answer the question.

choices.note: Tests whether the populations differ genetically, which the original experiment already covered. Calcium isn’t varied.
Tempting, because cue concentration is the other worry in the same sentence. But this varies the crab cue, not calcium.
Waves, not calcium. And it compares spots within one bay.
CORRECT. Calcium is the only thing that changes, and crab cues are kept out. Any shell difference would show calcium’s effect.
Shell calcium tells you what shells are made of, not whether the water’s calcium makes shells thicker.
