questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question Ambler’s explanation of the difference in shell thickness between the periwinkles of the two bays?
choices: In a third bay on the Varn Peninsula where the shell-crushing crab is also common, periwinkles likewise have thick shells.
Crab cues in the open waters of Hesk Sound are everywhere far too dilute to cause any measurable change in periwinkle shells.
Periwinkles on Hesk Sound’s exposed headlands are more often dislodged by storm waves than are those living in its sheltered coves.
In Ambler’s tanks, thick-shelled periwinkles were more likely than thin-shelled periwinkles to survive attacks by crabs of the same size.
The water of Tolley Inlet contains less dissolved calcium than that of Hesk Sound, and periwinkles raised in low-calcium water build somewhat thinner shells.
questions.explanation: Ambler’s explanation needs wild Hesk Sound snails to be exposed to enough crab cue to trigger thickening; the fourth paragraph already worries that tank concentrations exceeded those in open water. If cue levels throughout the sound are too low to have any effect, her mechanism cannot be what thickens the wild shells, so B seriously undermines it. E is the trap: it adds a possible contributing factor, which the author already allows, without showing that crab cues do not also work. A and D support Ambler, and C is irrelevant to the cue account.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most damages the crab-cue explanation of the wild difference.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Fourth paragraph, second sentence (cue concentrations, calcium), and the last sentence of the second paragraph (her hypothesis).

breakdown.analysis: Ambler’s experiment shows snails can respond to crab cues in tanks. Her explanation says that’s why wild Hesk Sound snails are thick. Gap: are wild snails actually exposed to enough cue? The author flags this: tank levels were “probably higher” than in open water. So attack that link. If the sound’s cue levels are too low to do anything, the tank result can’t explain the wild pattern. It’s like proving a drug works at ten times the dose people actually take.

choices.note: Strengthens. Another crab bay with thick shells fits Ambler’s pattern.
CORRECT. If wild cue levels are below the threshold for any effect, crab cues can’t be what makes Hesk Sound shells thick, whatever happens in tanks.
Irrelevant. Dislodging rates don’t bear on what controls shell thickness, and Ambler already showed sheltered and exposed shells are alike.
Strengthens the logic of her account: thick shells really are useful against crabs.

Tempting, since calcium is the alternative the author mentions. But it shows only that calcium may contribute a little (“somewhat thinner”). Both factors could operate, so Ambler’s crab account survives. B, by contrast, removes her mechanism entirely.

questions.stimulus: Film critic: Many viewers assume that a remake exists only to cash in on the reputation of the original film. Some remakes surely do. But the new remake of the thriller Glass Harbor deserves to be watched on its own merits. Its director moved the story from a crowded city to a remote fishing village, and that change gives the familiar plot a sense of isolation the original never had. Admittedly, the remake’s dialogue is weaker than the original’s.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the film critic’s argument?
choices: Many remakes exist only to cash in on the reputation of the original film.
The remake of Glass Harbor has weaker dialogue than the original film has.
The remake of Glass Harbor is worth watching for its own qualities.
Moving a story to a new setting can give a familiar plot qualities the original lacked.
The remake of Glass Harbor is a better film than the original Glass Harbor.
questions.explanation: The critic grants that some remakes are cash-ins and that this one’s dialogue is weaker, but argues that the new setting makes the Glass Harbor remake worth watching on its own merits, which C restates. E is tempting, but the critic never ranks the remake above the original; a film can be worth watching without being better.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new Glass Harbor remake deserves to be watched on its own merits.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Its new fishing-village setting gives the plot an isolation the original lacked (support); some remakes are cash-ins and its dialogue is weaker (concessions).

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The first sentence is a popular view, and ‘Some remakes surely do’ is a concession to it. ‘But’ flips to the critic’s own view: this remake is worth watching for itself. The setting change is the reason given for that. The ‘Admittedly’ sentence is another concession. We need an answer that says the remake deserves to be watched on its own merits.

choices.note: This is the popular view the critic pushes back on. The critic even grants that some remakes are like this, but that’s a concession, not the point.
This is the ‘Admittedly’ concession. Concessions are things the author grants despite the conclusion, not the conclusion itself.

CORRECT. ‘Worth watching for its own qualities’ is just a restatement of ‘deserves to be watched on its own merits.’ The setting change supports it; the other sentences are background and concessions.
Too general, and it’s a premise. The critic says this particular setting change helped this particular film. That supports the conclusion; it isn’t the conclusion.

Tempting. It sounds like a fan’s verdict. But the critic never compares the films overall, and even admits the dialogue is worse. ‘Worth watching’ isn’t ‘better than the original.’ Watch for unsupported rankings.

questions.stimulus: Gardening columnist: A survey of home gardeners in our region found that those who keep a written log of what they plant and when they water harvest, on average, considerably more vegetables per square meter than those who keep no such log. Clearly, keeping a garden log makes a gardener more productive, so anyone who wants a bigger harvest should start one.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the gardening columnist’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: overlooks the possibility that gardeners who are more diligent in general are more likely to keep a log
presumes, without providing justification, that gardeners who keep logs record their planting and watering dates accurately
takes for granted that a larger harvest is the only reason that a gardener might have for keeping a written log
draws a conclusion about every vegetable grown in the region from the harvests of only some kinds of vegetables
relies on a survey of gardeners without establishing that the people who conducted it are experts in gardening
questions.explanation: The columnist moves from a correlation (log keepers harvest more) to a cause (the log makes them more productive), ignoring that diligent gardeners may both keep logs and tend their plots better; A names that overlooked alternative. B is tempting, but whether the logs are accurate has nothing to do with whether keeping one causes bigger harvests.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Keeping a garden log makes a gardener more productive (so anyone wanting a bigger harvest should keep one).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Gardeners who keep logs harvest more per square meter than gardeners who don’t.

breakdown.analysis: So log keepers grow more. Does the log do it? Think about who bothers to write down every planting and watering. Careful, committed gardeners. Those same people weed, water on time and fix problems early. The log could just be a sign of a diligent gardener, not the cause of the harvest. It’s like saying people who own running watches are fitter, so buying a running watch makes you fit. We need an answer that says some other trait could explain both the log and the bigger harvest.

choices.note: CORRECT. This is the classic correlation-to-causation gap. Diligence could produce both the log and the harvest, so the log itself may do nothing.
Tempting, because a sloppy log sounds useless. But the argument isn’t about what’s written in the log. Even perfectly accurate logs wouldn’t show the log causes bigger harvests.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Students who keep diaries remember the year better, because their diaries record the year correctly.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The columnist never says why people keep logs. The claim is about what logs do, not about gardeners’ motives.
Not this argument’s problem. The survey measured vegetables per square meter overall, and the conclusion is about productivity in general, not every kind of vegetable.
Attacks the source. Who ran the survey doesn’t matter much; the flaw is in the inference drawn from its results. Answers that attack the source are usually traps.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The study showing that seat belts save lives was run by statisticians, not drivers, so we can ignore it.

questions.stimulus:
Ilse: Kelso’s town council should drop its rule that every new house include two off-street parking spaces. The rule adds thousands of dollars to the price of each new house, and many buyers own just one car.

Marco: Dropping the rule would push hundreds more cars onto Kelso’s narrow streets, which already leave snowplows barely enough room each winter. The rule should stay, even if it does make new houses cost more.
questions.stem: Ilse and Marco disagree over whether
choices: the parking rule adds to the price of the new houses built in Kelso
many of the people who buy new houses in Kelso own only a single car
Kelso’s town council should drop its rule requiring off-street parking for new houses
snowplows in Kelso would be unable to clear the town’s streets if more cars were parked on them
the price of new housing should be the main consideration when a town decides which building rules to adopt
questions.explanation: Ilse says the parking rule should be dropped; Marco says it should stay, so they disagree about C. They agree on A, since Marco concedes the rule makes houses cost more, and D and B are each addressed by only one speaker.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ilse: drop the two-space parking rule, because it raises house prices and many buyers own one car; Marco: keep the rule, because dropping it would crowd Kelso’s narrow streets, even though it raises costs.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Line them up. Should the rule be dropped? Ilse: yes. Marco: no (‘The rule should stay’). Does the rule raise prices? Ilse: yes. Marco: yes too (‘even if it does make new houses cost more’). That’s agreement. Everything else is something only one of them talks about. We need the answer about dropping the rule.

choices.note: They agree on this. Ilse says the rule adds thousands of dollars, and Marco concedes it makes new houses cost more. Agreement isn’t disagreement.
Only Ilse mentions one-car buyers. Marco never says how many cars buyers own, so we can’t say he disagrees.
CORRECT. Ilse says the council should drop the rule. Marco says the rule should stay. Both commit, in opposite directions.
Only Marco talks about the streets and snowplows, and even he says only that plows barely have room now. Ilse says nothing about it.
Neither speaker says this. Ilse cites price as one reason, but never calls it the main consideration, and Marco explicitly weighs it against crowded streets.

questions.stimulus: To save money, the Ashford recreation department plans to end the evening van service that takes older residents home after classes at the community center. But many of the older residents who attend these evening classes have no other way to get home. So ending the van service will reduce attendance at the center’s evening classes.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: The van service costs the recreation department more each year than any of its other programs for older residents does.
Not all of the attendees who have no other way home would keep attending if the van service ended.
Evening classes are more valuable to older residents than the money saved by ending the van service is to the department.
Most of the people who attend evening classes at the community center are older residents who have no other way home.
The recreation department has no other way to save as much money as it would save by ending the van service.
questions.explanation: The argument moves from ‘many attendees have no other ride home’ to ‘attendance will fall,’ which requires that at least some of those people would actually stop coming; B says this modestly. D is too strong: the argument needs only some dropouts, not that most attendees lack a ride.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Ending the van service will reduce attendance at evening classes.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Many older residents who attend have no other way to get home.

breakdown.analysis: Having no ride home is a problem. But does it actually make people stop coming? Maybe they’d walk, or tough it out, or a neighbor would start driving them. The argument needs at least some of these people to drop out. We need an answer that says not every one of them would keep attending. Notice the hedge: ‘not all’ is the kind of minimal answer a required assumption usually is.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The van’s cost compared with other programs has nothing to do with whether attendance falls.
choices.negation: The van service does not cost more than every other program for older residents.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it and the argument dies: if all of them would keep coming anyway, attendance doesn’t fall.
choices.negation: All of the attendees who have no other way home would keep attending if the van service ended.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. This weighs value against savings, which matters for whether the plan is wise. The argument only predicts attendance.
choices.negation: Evening classes are not more valuable to older residents than the savings are to the department.

choices.note: Too strong. ‘Many’ riders dropping out is enough to lower attendance; they don’t need to be most of the class.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most attendees are older residents with no other way home.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Other ways to save money bear on whether the plan is a good idea, not on what it will do to attendance.
choices.negation: The department has some other way to save as much money.

questions.stimulus: In the Merrow River, young salmon released from a hatchery survive to adulthood at a much lower rate than young salmon hatched in the wild. Hatchery salmon are fed by hand until their release and so have had little experience avoiding predators. Fisheries biologists therefore conclude that the hatchery salmon’s lower survival rate is due largely to their inexperience with predators.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the biologists’ argument?
choices: Wild salmon in the Merrow River are, on average, slightly larger at a given age than hatchery salmon are.
The number of predatory fish in the Merrow River has risen steadily over the past decade, according to a recent survey.
Some of the hatchery salmon released into the Merrow River survive to adulthood even though they were fed by hand.
Hatchery salmon briefly exposed to predatory fish in holding ponds before release survived at nearly the wild salmon’s rate.
Hatchery salmon are caught by anglers more often than wild salmon are, because anglers favor the stretch of river near the hatchery.
questions.explanation: If inexperience with predators is the cause, giving hatchery salmon some predator experience should close the survival gap, and D reports exactly that. E is tempting because it is about why hatchery salmon die, but it supplies a different cause (anglers), which weakens rather than strengthens the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Hatchery salmon survive less well mainly because they lack experience avoiding predators.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Hatchery salmon survive to adulthood less often than wild salmon; hatchery salmon are hand-fed and have little predator experience.

breakdown.analysis: Is predator inexperience really the cause? Hatchery fish differ from wild fish in lots of ways: size, genes, where they’re released. To strengthen a causal claim, look for an answer that isolates the proposed cause: change only the predator experience and see whether survival changes. It’s like testing whether a kid is failing math because he skips homework: make him do the homework and see whether his grades go up. We need an answer that says giving hatchery fish predator experience improves their survival.

choices.note: This points to a different difference between the groups: size. If anything it suggests another cause of the gap, so it doesn’t help the biologist.
More predators would affect wild and hatchery salmon alike. A survey of predator numbers doesn’t explain why one group survives worse than the other.
So? Some hatchery survivors are expected even if the group does worse overall. This says nothing about why the rates differ.
CORRECT. This is the controlled test. Same hatchery fish, plus predator experience, and the survival gap nearly disappears. That points right at inexperience as the cause.
Tempting, because it’s about why hatchery salmon die. But it names a different cause, anglers near the hatchery. That’s an alternative explanation, so it weakens the argument.

questions.stimulus: Last year the regional airline Talmor Air replaced the seats in its turboprop planes, which fly short mountain routes, with thinner, lighter seats. In surveys, passengers consistently rate the new seats as less comfortable than the old ones. Yet over the year after the change, Talmor’s passenger satisfaction scores for its turboprop flights rose substantially.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why Talmor’s satisfaction scores for its turboprop flights rose?
choices: Talmor’s competitors on the same mountain routes did not replace the seats in their own turboprop planes that year.
Passengers on short flights generally care less about seat comfort than passengers on long flights do.
The new seats cost Talmor less to buy and maintain than the old seats did, which lowered its operating costs.
Satisfaction scores for Talmor’s jet flights, whose seats were not replaced, did not change at all over the same year.
Because the new seats are lighter, Talmor’s turboprops now rarely have to leave checked bags behind to meet weight limits.
questions.explanation: The lighter seats had a side benefit passengers notice: their bags now travel with them, which can outweigh a less comfortable seat on a short flight; E explains the rise. B is tempting, but caring less about comfort would at most keep scores from falling; it gives no reason for them to rise.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Talmor put in seats passengers find less comfortable, but satisfaction with its turboprop flights went up.

breakdown.analysis: How does a worse seat lead to happier passengers? Look for something else the new seats did. Here the clue is in the stimulus: the seats are lighter, and the planes fly short mountain routes. Weight might matter. The defect (thin seats) could come bundled with a benefit. We need an answer that shows the change produced some gain passengers value more than seat comfort.

choices.note: So? What competitors did doesn’t explain why Talmor’s own passengers became more satisfied with flights that got worse seats.
Tempting. It softens the blow of the worse seats. But ‘cares less’ only explains why scores might not drop much. It gives no reason for them to go up.
Wrong dimension. Lower costs for Talmor explain why the airline made the change, not why passengers were happier.
This makes the puzzle sharper, not smaller. It rules out a general rise across the airline but provides no explanation for the turboprop increase.
CORRECT. The lighter seats mean bags stop getting left behind. Passengers hate losing their bags more than they mind a thinner seat on a short hop, so satisfaction rises.

questions.stimulus: Customers at the Linley post office often wait twenty minutes or more in line during the lunch hour. To shorten these waits, the postmaster plans to staff a second service window during that hour. Since two clerks can serve customers twice as fast as one clerk can, the plan should cut lunch-hour waits roughly in half.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Most lunch-hour delays occur while parcels are weighed on the office’s single scale, which both windows would have to share.
Many customers who come to the post office during the lunch hour are buying only stamps, which takes a minute or two.
The clerk who would staff the second window currently sorts incoming mail in the back room during the lunch hour.
Customers at other post offices in the region report waiting in line for even longer than customers at the Linley office do.
The Linley post office has more customers during the lunch hour than during any other hour of the day.
questions.explanation: The prediction assumes that clerks are the bottleneck; A shows the real bottleneck is the single scale, which a second window can’t double, so waits won’t fall by half. C is tempting because it names a cost of the plan, but moving a sorting clerk says nothing about whether lines get shorter.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Adding a second window should cut lunch-hour waits roughly in half.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Two clerks can serve customers twice as fast as one.

breakdown.analysis: Two clerks serve twice as fast only if the clerk is what slows things down. What if something else is the choke point? Picture a grocery store that opens a second register but has only one bagger who has to bag every order. The lines barely move faster. We need an answer showing that the delay comes from something a second window doesn’t fix.

choices.note: CORRECT. If most of the wait is spent at the one scale, a second clerk just means two people waiting for the same scale. The doubling math breaks down.
If anything this helps. Quick stamp sales are exactly what an extra clerk speeds through. It doesn’t show the plan will fail.
Tempting, because it’s a real downside: the back room loses a sorter. But the argument is only about lunch-hour lines, and this doesn’t touch them.
Irrelevant comparison. Waits elsewhere being worse doesn’t tell us whether Linley’s plan will shorten Linley’s lines.
This just confirms that lunch is the busy hour, which is why the plan targets it. It doesn’t show the extra window won’t help.

questions.stimulus: Under Wendmoor Insurance’s homeowner policy, a claim for water damage is paid only if the damage was reported within thirty days. Moreover, any claim for water damage caused by a burst pipe is paid in full, provided that the damage was reported within thirty days and the home’s pipes had been professionally inspected within the preceding five years. The Delgado family’s claim for water damage caused by a burst pipe was paid, but not in full.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: The Delgados reported the water damage to Wendmoor more than thirty days after it occurred.
Wendmoor pays claims in full only when the water damage was caused by a burst pipe.
The Delgados’ pipes had not been professionally inspected within the five years before the damage.
Some claims for water damage that was not caused by a burst pipe are paid in full by Wendmoor.
Wendmoor would have refused the Delgados’ claim entirely if their pipes had not been inspected within the preceding five years.
questions.explanation: Because the claim was paid at all, the damage was reported within thirty days; it was a burst pipe; so if the pipes had been inspected within five years it would have been paid in full. It wasn’t, so the inspection condition failed, as C says. A is the reversal trap: being paid proves the report was timely.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Water claim paid → reported within 30 days; 2. Burst pipe AND reported within 30 days AND inspected within 5 years → paid in full; 3. Delgados: burst pipe, claim paid, not in full.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Paid → reported within 30 days. So the Delgados reported on time. They had a burst pipe. Rule 2: burst pipe + on time + inspected → paid in full. Contrapositive: not paid in full → not burst pipe OR not on time OR not inspected. They had a burst pipe and reported on time, so the only condition left to fail is the inspection. We need: the pipes weren’t inspected within five years.

choices.note: This reverses the facts. The claim was paid, and payment requires a report within thirty days. So they must have reported on time.
We don’t know this. The policy gives one route to full payment; it never says burst pipes are the only route.
CORRECT. Burst pipe and an on-time report (proven by payment) plus an inspection would have guaranteed full payment. They didn’t get full payment, so the inspection piece is missing.
We don’t know this. The policy says nothing about full payment for other kinds of water damage. Could be true; doesn’t have to be.
Contradicted. Their pipes weren’t inspected, and their claim was still paid in part. So lacking an inspection doesn’t mean total refusal.

questions.stimulus: In a recent study, researchers asked 200 adults to describe aloud the most stressful car trip they had ever taken, and they recorded the participants’ hand movements as they spoke. Seventy percent of the participants gestured with their hands at least once while doing so. This shows that recounting stressful experiences tends to make people gesture.
questions.stem: The argument’s reasoning is flawed in that the argument
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that the participants found the trips they described to be equally stressful
draws a conclusion about people in general from a sample of participants that is too small to be meaningful
takes for granted that people remember the details of stressful experiences accurately when they describe them
confuses a possible cause of gesturing while speaking with a possible effect of gesturing while speaking
fails to establish how often the participants gesture when describing experiences that were not stressful
questions.explanation: To show that stressful memories in particular bring out gesturing, the argument needs a baseline: if people gesture just as often describing their grocery list, the stress did nothing. E names the missing comparison. B is tempting, but 200 participants is not obviously too few, and even a huge sample would not supply the baseline.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Recounting stressful experiences tends to make people gesture.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 70 percent of 200 adults gestured at least once while describing their most stressful car trip.

breakdown.analysis: Seventy percent gestured. Compared to what? Most people wave their hands around when they talk about anything. If 70 percent also gesture when describing breakfast, stress has nothing to do with it. This is a missing comparison group: the study only looked at one kind of story. It’s like noting that most people blink while watching horror movies and concluding horror movies make people blink. We need an answer that points to the missing baseline.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The trips don’t have to be equally stressful. The conclusion is about stressful stories in general, not about matching stress levels.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Everyone in the race finished, so all the runners must be equally fit.

choices.note: Tempting. Sample-size complaints are a reflex. But 200 people is a respectable sample, and the real issue isn’t size; it’s that there’s nothing to compare against.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: I asked three friends and they all liked the movie, so everyone will.

choices.note: Memory accuracy doesn’t matter. The study measured gesturing while people talked, which happens whether or not their memories are correct.
Describes a different flaw. The argument doesn’t mix up cause and effect; no one suggests gesturing causes stressful memories.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: People who carry umbrellas get rained on more, so carrying umbrellas causes rain.

choices.note: CORRECT. Without knowing how often people gesture when talking about non-stressful things, 70 percent tells us nothing about stress. That’s the missing baseline.

questions.stimulus: Railway spokesperson: Two years ago Daventry Rail replaced fixed-schedule servicing of its trains with inspections triggered by sensor data. Since then, our train crews have reported 30 percent fewer equipment malfunctions per thousand trips than they did before. Clearly, the new maintenance program has made travel on Daventry’s trains safer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the spokesperson’s argument?
choices: Since the new program was adopted, Daventry’s trains have been running longer routes, on average, than they did before.
Other railways that adopted maintenance programs similar to Daventry’s also saw declines in the number of reported malfunctions.
Under the new program, brake and signal malfunctions have become more frequent, while heating and door malfunctions have dropped sharply.
The new maintenance program costs Daventry considerably more each year than its previous program did, mostly because of the sensors.
Both before and after the new program was adopted, some Daventry crews failed to report minor malfunctions to the maintenance staff.
questions.explanation: The argument measures safety by the number of malfunctions, but safety depends on which malfunctions occur; C shows the dangerous ones rose while minor ones fell, so fewer total malfunctions does not mean safer trains. E is tempting, but underreporting that happened both before and after cannot explain the change.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new maintenance program has made Daventry’s trains safer.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Reported equipment malfunctions per thousand trips fell 30 percent after the program began.

breakdown.analysis: Is the number of malfunctions really the measure of safety? A stuck heater and a failing brake each count as one malfunction. If the small stuff went down and the serious stuff went up, the total drops while the trains get more dangerous. This is a count-versus-severity mismatch. We need an answer that says the decline came from trivial malfunctions while dangerous ones didn’t fall (or rose).

choices.note: Longer routes give more chances for something to break per trip. If malfunctions per trip still fell, the program looks even better. Not a weakener.
This strengthens. If similar programs elsewhere also cut malfunctions, the program likely did something here too.
CORRECT. The total fell because heaters and doors broke less, but brake and signal problems, the ones that matter for safety, became more common. Fewer malfunctions, less safety.
Wrong dimension. Cost has nothing to do with whether the trains are safer.
Tempting, because underreporting can distort numbers. But it happened both before and after, so it can’t explain the drop. A constant problem doesn’t create a change.

questions.stimulus: In the Kaleni language, a word borrowed from another language keeps its original stress pattern for at least a generation after it enters Kaleni. Every native Kaleni word, by contrast, is stressed on its first syllable. The common Kaleni word ‘kelmaro’ is stressed on its second syllable.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: The word ‘kelmaro’ entered the Kaleni language at some point within the past generation.
The word ‘kelmaro’ did not originate in the Kaleni language itself.
Most of the words that have been borrowed into Kaleni are stressed on their second syllable.
Borrowed words that have been part of Kaleni for more than a generation are stressed on their first syllable.
‘Kelmaro’ was borrowed from a language in which it was stressed on its second syllable.
questions.explanation: Native words are always stressed on the first syllable; ‘kelmaro’ is not, so it cannot be native, as B says. A and D misread ‘at least a generation’: borrowed words keep their stress for a generation or longer, so a word stressed on its second syllable may have been borrowed long ago, and nothing says older borrowings shift.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Borrowed word → keeps original stress for at least a generation; 2. Native Kaleni word → stressed on first syllable; 3. ‘Kelmaro’ is stressed on its second syllable.

breakdown.analysis: Start with the cleanest rule. Native → first-syllable stress. Contrapositive: not first-syllable stress → not native. Kelmaro is stressed on the second syllable, so it isn’t native. Done. Watch the phrase ‘at least a generation.’ It sets a minimum, not a maximum. It doesn’t say what happens after a generation, so answers about timing or later stress changes are unsupported.

choices.note: Tempting. It feels like a borrowed word that still has odd stress must be recent. But ‘at least a generation’ means borrowed words may keep their stress much longer. Kelmaro could be centuries old.
CORRECT. Native words are always first-syllable stressed. Kelmaro isn’t, so it isn’t native: it didn’t originate in Kaleni. This one actually must be true.
We don’t know this. One second-syllable word tells us nothing about most borrowed words.
Reads a maximum into a minimum. The stimulus never says borrowed words shift after a generation; they keep their stress for at least that long, maybe forever.

We don’t know this. Kelmaro isn’t native, but if it was borrowed long ago its stress could have shifted, and it might not even be borrowed (it could, for example, have been formed some other way). Its original stress is unknown.

questions.stimulus: School board member: The district’s cafeteria vendor has proposed adding flavored milk to the lunch menu, noting that students would drink more milk if it were offered. Flavored milk does supply calcium, which growing children need. But it also contains a considerable amount of added sugar, and many parents have told the board they do not want their children offered sugary drinks at school. So we should decline the vendor’s proposal.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the school board member’s reasoning?
choices: A school should offer students whatever nutritious foods they are most likely to consume, regardless of any other concerns that are raised.
Decisions about school menus should be based solely on nutritional considerations, never on the preferences that parents happen to express.
A food that supplies a nutrient children need should be offered at school even if the food contains some added sugar.
A school should not offer a food that many parents object to on health grounds, even if the food is nutritious.
A school should accept a vendor’s proposal only if the vendor can show that students would benefit from the proposed change.
questions.explanation: The member concedes that flavored milk has a nutritional benefit but declines it because many parents object to sugary drinks; D says exactly that parental health objections override some nutritional value. E is tempting, but the vendor arguably did show a benefit (more milk, more calcium), so E would not tell the board to decline.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The board should decline the proposal to add flavored milk.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Flavored milk supplies calcium (concession) but has added sugar; many parents don’t want sugary drinks offered to their children at school.

breakdown.analysis: Why say no to milk that kids would actually drink? Because of the sugar and the parents’ objections, even granting the calcium. A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says: decline. And it should fit the reasons: parent objections on health grounds beat a nutritional upside. We need a rule like: when many parents object to a food for health reasons, don’t offer it, even if it has some benefit.

choices.note: This points the other way. Students would drink more flavored milk, and it’s nutritious in part, so this rule supports offering it.
This throws out the parents’ objections, which are the heart of the member’s reasoning. It doesn’t lead to declining.
Opposite. This would tell the board to offer flavored milk, since it supplies calcium.

CORRECT. Many parents object on health grounds (sugar), and the rule says don’t offer the food even though it’s nutritious (calcium). Every piece of the argument is covered, and the rule tells the board to decline.
Tempting. It sounds cautious. But the vendor pointed to a benefit, more milk and so more calcium, so this rule might even favor accepting. It doesn’t use the sugar or the parents at all.

questions.stimulus: Brookvale homes equipped with smoke detectors that are wired into the house’s electrical system are more likely to suffer serious fire damage than are Brookvale homes that have only battery-powered detectors. Yet Brookvale’s fire officials insist that wired detectors are more reliable than battery-powered ones and that nearly every home would be safer with them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Brookvale requires wired detectors in every home with a wood stove or fireplace, the source of most serious fires there.
Battery-powered detectors in Brookvale homes are often found during inspections to have dead or missing batteries.
Wired detectors cost considerably more to install than battery-powered detectors do, though they cost less to maintain over time.
Unlike battery-powered detectors, wired detectors keep working without depending on homeowners to remember to replace their batteries.
Most serious house fires in Brookvale begin at night, when residents are asleep and depend on a detector’s alarm to wake them.
questions.explanation: If wired detectors are required precisely in the homes most prone to serious fires, those homes would suffer more damage even if the detectors work better, so A lets both facts stand. D is tempting, but it only supports the officials’ side; it does nothing to explain why homes with wired detectors fare worse.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Homes with wired detectors suffer more serious fire damage, but officials say wired detectors are more reliable and would make homes safer.

breakdown.analysis: How can the better detector go with worse outcomes? Ask who has the wired detectors. If they’re installed mostly in homes that are far more likely to catch fire, those homes could have more damage even though the detector helps. It’s like noticing that people with the best doctors are often the sickest: the sick people seek out the best doctors. We need an answer that shows the wired-detector homes differ in fire risk. Watch for answers that explain only one side.

choices.note: CORRECT. Wired detectors are concentrated in the riskiest homes. Those homes have more serious fires to begin with, so they show more damage even if the detectors are better. Both facts survive.
This deepens the puzzle. If battery detectors often don’t work, the homes relying on them should do worse, not better.
Wrong dimension. Installation and maintenance costs say nothing about fire damage or reliability.
Tempting. It backs up the officials’ reliability claim. But it explains only one side; it gives no reason the wired-detector homes suffer more damage.
This applies to every home, wired or not. A fact about all homes can’t explain a difference between two groups of them.

questions.stimulus: Choir director: The Oldham Choral Society should keep holding its concerts at St. Bride’s Hall. Some members want to move them to the new civic auditorium, which seats twice as many people. But our audiences have never filled even St. Bride’s, and the auditorium’s acoustics flatten unamplified voices. Thus, a move would leave the choir sounding worse to no more listeners than before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the choir director’s argument by the claim that a move would leave the choir sounding worse to no more listeners than before?
choices: It is the overall conclusion that the choir director’s argument as a whole is intended to establish.
It is a conclusion drawn from other claims in the argument and offered in support of its main conclusion.
It is a premise that some members of the society offer in support of moving the concerts to the auditorium.
It is a claim that the choir director concedes is true but argues is outweighed by other considerations.
It is a general principle that the choir director applies to the particular case of the society’s concerts.
questions.explanation: The claim is drawn (‘Thus’) from the facts about audience size and acoustics, and it in turn supports the opening recommendation to stay at St. Bride’s, so B is right. A is the trap: the ‘Thus’ marks a conclusion, but not the main one; the claim is the reason the society should keep its concerts where they are.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The society should keep holding its concerts at St. Bride’s Hall.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Audiences never fill St. Bride’s and the auditorium flattens voices; so a move would mean worse sound for no more listeners (the claim in question).

breakdown.analysis: Ask which statement supports which. The conclusion is the one everything else supports. The claim starts with ‘Thus,’ so it’s a conclusion of something: the facts about audiences and acoustics. But does the argument stop there? No. Why should the society stay? Because moving would make it sound worse to the same crowd. So the claim supports the first sentence. Chain: audience and acoustics facts → worse sound, no more listeners → stay at St. Bride’s. That makes it an intermediate conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting, because of the ‘Thus.’ But the main conclusion sits in the first sentence with no indicator: keep the concerts at St. Bride’s. This claim is the reason for it.
CORRECT. It’s supported by the audience and acoustics facts, and it supports the recommendation to stay. Drawn from premises, used as a premise.
Wrong side. The members who want to move would never say the move makes the choir sound worse. This is the director’s own claim against them.
The director doesn’t concede this; the director asserts it and relies on it. Nothing outweighs it.
It’s about one specific move for one choir. That’s a particular claim, not a general principle.

questions.stimulus: Hospital administrator: Some of our staff propose installing hand-sanitizer stations outside every patient room to reduce the number of infections that patients acquire in our hospital. But studies of hospitals like ours show that most such infections are spread by contaminated equipment, not by the hands of staff or visitors. So installing the stations would not be worthwhile.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the hospital administrator’s argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: takes for granted that studies of other hospitals accurately describe how infections are spread in every hospital in the country
presumes, without providing justification, that staff members would not use the sanitizer stations if they were installed
confuses the number of infections spread by equipment with the severity of the infections that equipment spreads
infers that a measure is not worthwhile from the fact that it would not address the main source of a problem
attacks the motives of the staff who proposed the stations rather than addressing the merits of their proposal
questions.explanation: Showing that hands spread only a minority of infections does not show that cutting hand-spread infections is not worth doing; D describes that leap. A is tempting, but the studies are of ‘hospitals like ours,’ and the argument never makes a claim about every hospital in the country.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Installing hand-sanitizer stations would not be worthwhile.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most hospital-acquired infections are spread by contaminated equipment, not by hands.

breakdown.analysis: So most infections come from equipment. Does that make the hand-borne ones not worth preventing? If hands spread, say, 40 percent of infections, cutting those would still prevent a lot of illness. A fix doesn’t have to solve the whole problem to be worth doing. It’s like refusing to fix a leaky window because most of your heat escapes through the roof. We need an answer that says the argument rejects a partial solution just because it isn’t the main one.

choices.note: Tempting, because relying on other hospitals’ studies sounds risky. But the administrator cites studies of ‘hospitals like ours’ and draws a conclusion only about this hospital, not every hospital in the country.
The argument never says or assumes staff would ignore the stations. Its reason is about where infections come from, not about usage.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We shouldn’t buy a treadmill, since we’d never use it (with no evidence about whether we would).

choices.note: Describes a different flaw. The administrator never mentions severity; the argument is about which route spreads most infections.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Most of our complaints are about slow service, so slow service must be our most serious problem.

choices.note: CORRECT. The stations would target a minority source, but that doesn’t make them worthless. The argument treats ‘not the main source’ as ‘not worth addressing.’
The administrator says nothing about the staff’s motives; the response addresses the proposal itself. Attacks-the-source answers are usually traps.

questions.stimulus: Every piece in the Arbel Quartet’s spring program is scored for harpsichord. A harpsichord piece can be performed at Wren Chapel only if the chapel’s old harpsichord is restored. So unless that harpsichord is restored, none of the pieces in the Arbel Quartet’s spring program can be performed at Wren Chapel.
questions.stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Every van in Mira’s delivery fleet runs on diesel. A diesel vehicle may enter the old town only if the city lifts its emissions ban. So unless the ban is lifted, none of Mira’s vans may enter the old town.

Every exhibit at the Corso Gallery that requires dim lighting is a textile. The gallery can display textiles only if its humidity system is working. So if the humidity system is working, all of the dim-lit exhibits can be displayed.

Every runner on the team trains on the school track, and the track can be used only if it has been resurfaced since the winter. The track has been resurfaced. So every runner on the team can use the track this season.

Some of the songs on the band’s new album were recorded in Studio 4. A song recorded in Studio 4 can be released only if the studio’s owner consents. So unless the owner consents, none of the songs on the album can be released.

Every apartment in the Marlow Building has a gas stove, and a gas stove can be installed only by a licensed fitter. So every licensed fitter in the city has installed at least one stove in the Marlow Building.
questions.explanation: The original is valid: all A are B; a B can do C only if D; so without D, no A can do C. A matches each step. D is the closest trap, but it starts from ‘some’ songs, so its ‘none of the songs’ conclusion does not follow, and B and C treat the necessary condition as if it were sufficient.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Unless the harpsichord is restored, none of the spring-program pieces can be performed at Wren Chapel.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every program piece is a harpsichord piece; a harpsichord piece can be performed at Wren only if the harpsichord is restored.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are B; B can do C only if D; so if not D, no A can do C.

breakdown.analysis: The original is valid. Program piece → harpsichord piece → (performed at Wren → harpsichord restored). Contrapositive: not restored → no harpsichord piece performed → no program piece performed. Match three things: an ‘all’ first premise, an ‘only if’ requirement, and a conclusion that denies the requirement and denies the outcome for the whole group. Watch for answers that turn the ‘only if’ into an ‘if’ or start from ‘some.’

choices.note: CORRECT. All vans are diesel (all A are B); a diesel may enter only if the ban is lifted (B does C only if D); so unless the ban is lifted, no van may enter (not D → no A does C). Step for step.
This flips the requirement into a guarantee. ‘Only if the humidity system works’ makes the system necessary, but the conclusion treats it as sufficient for display.
Same mistake as B. Resurfacing is required for using the track; this treats it as enough. It also adds a fact premise the original doesn’t have.
Tempting. The wording matches the original almost exactly. But it starts with ‘some’ songs, so it can’t conclude that ‘none of the songs’ can be released. Songs recorded elsewhere might be fine.
Not even close. It jumps from ‘stoves need licensed fitters’ to ‘every fitter installed one here.’ That’s a different, badly flawed argument.

questions.stimulus: Archaeologist: Any pottery fragment that bears traces of lead glaze was made after the end of the Varn period, since potters in this region learned lead glazing only from traders who arrived at the very end of that period. The pottery fragments found in the lowest layer of the dig at Osk Hill bear traces of lead glaze. Therefore, the lowest layer at Osk Hill was deposited after the Varn period ended.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the archaeologist’s argument can be properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every pottery fragment that was made after the end of the Varn period bears traces of lead glaze.
Any layer of a dig that contains pottery made after the Varn period was deposited after that period ended.
The traders who introduced lead glazing to the region settled at Osk Hill near the end of the Varn period.
Pottery fragments found in the lowest layer of a dig are usually the oldest fragments found anywhere at that dig.
No pottery made during the Varn period has been found in any of the layers of the dig at Osk Hill.
questions.explanation: The premises establish only that the lowest layer’s fragments were made after the Varn period; B links fragments to the layer, so the layer’s date follows. A reverses the conditional about glaze, and D says only what is usually true of lowest layers, so neither guarantees the conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The lowest layer at Osk Hill was deposited after the Varn period.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lead-glazed fragment → made after the Varn period; the lowest layer’s fragments are lead-glazed.

breakdown.analysis: Chain what we have: lowest-layer fragments → lead-glazed → made after Varn. But the conclusion is about when the layer was deposited, not when the pottery was made. Could fragments made later get into an older layer? Burrowing animals, later digging. The missing link is: layer contains post-Varn fragments → layer deposited post-Varn. Full chain: lowest-layer fragments → glazed → made after Varn → (assumption) layer deposited after Varn. We need that bridge from the fragments’ date to the layer’s date.

choices.note: This reverses the conditional. We already know glazed → after Varn. Knowing after Varn → glazed adds nothing about when the layer was deposited.
CORRECT. The lowest layer contains fragments made after Varn, and this rule says any such layer was deposited after Varn. The conclusion follows exactly.
Irrelevant. Where the traders lived doesn’t connect the fragments’ date to the layer’s date.
Tempting, since it’s about the lowest layer. But ‘usually the oldest’ doesn’t tell us the layer was laid down after the fragments were made, and ‘usually’ can’t guarantee anything.
So? Finding no Varn-period pottery doesn’t show when the lowest layer was deposited. The layer could still predate the glazed fragments that ended up in it.

questions.stimulus: Ambrose Mutual offers its auto-insurance customers an optional dashboard monitor that beeps whenever the driver brakes harshly or accelerates sharply. Last year, Ambrose drivers who had installed the monitor filed 25 percent fewer accident claims than Ambrose drivers who had not. Ambrose’s analysts conclude that using the monitor makes people drive more safely.
questions.stem: The answer to which one of the following questions would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the analysts’ argument?
choices: How much does Ambrose Mutual charge the customers who choose to install the dashboard monitor in their cars?
Do any other auto insurers in the region offer their customers a monitor similar to the one Ambrose offers?
Are claims for accidents more costly for Ambrose to pay, on average, than the other kinds of claims it receives?
Did Ambrose drivers without the monitor file more accident claims last year than they had in previous years?
Before installing the monitor, did the drivers who chose it file fewer accident claims than other Ambrose drivers?
questions.explanation: Drivers chose to install the monitor, so they may simply have been safer drivers to begin with; whether they already filed fewer claims before installing it decides whether the monitor deserves the credit, which is why E is useful. D is tempting, but last year’s comparison between the two groups is unaffected by whether the non-monitor group did better or worse than in earlier years.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Using the monitor makes people drive more safely.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Last year, Ambrose drivers with the optional monitor filed 25 percent fewer accident claims than those without.

breakdown.analysis: Who installs an optional safety beeper? Probably careful drivers. If the monitor group was already safer before getting it, the monitor didn’t cause the difference; the type of driver did. This is a self-selected group. An evaluate question wants a question whose answer cuts both ways: one answer helps, the other hurts. We need a question about whether the monitor users were already safer before they installed it.

choices.note: Wrong dimension. Price doesn’t tell us whether the monitor changes driving. Either answer leaves the argument where it was.
Irrelevant. Other insurers’ products don’t affect whether Ambrose’s monitor makes its drivers safer.
Irrelevant. Cost to Ambrose of a claim says nothing about whether the monitor reduces accidents.

Tempting, because it involves a before-and-after comparison. But the argument compares the two groups last year. Whether the no-monitor group got worse or better over time doesn’t explain the gap between groups.
CORRECT. If yes, the monitor users were already safer drivers, and self-selection, not the monitor, explains the gap. If no, the monitor looks like the real cause. Either answer matters.

questions.stimulus: Linguist: It is often said that text messaging is eroding young people’s ability to spell, since their messages are full of abbreviations such as ‘thx’ and ‘l8r.’ But to shorten a word deliberately in such ways, a writer must know how the full word is normally spelled and how it sounds. And studies find that the students who use such abbreviations most often tend to score at least as well on spelling tests as students who rarely use them. Thus, ______.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the linguist’s argument?
choices: students who send many text messages will gradually lose their ability to spell even common words correctly
frequent text messaging actually improves young people’s ability to spell the words they abbreviate
frequent use of texting abbreviations is not, by itself, a sign that a young person spells poorly
students who rarely send text messages tend to score worse on spelling tests than students who often do
abbreviations in text messages are harder for young people to produce than the conventionally spelled words they replace
questions.explanation: The linguist pushes back on the popular view by arguing that abbreviating requires knowing the spelling and that heavy abbreviators spell at least as well as others; the modest conclusion that abbreviating is not itself a sign of poor spelling, C, follows. B is the attractive overreach: the evidence shows no deficit, not that texting causes improvement.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Popular view: texting abbreviations erode spelling; 2. Deliberate abbreviating requires knowing the normal spelling and sound; 3. Heavy abbreviators score at least as well on spelling tests as light users.

breakdown.analysis: The ‘But’ tells you the linguist is pushing back on the popular view, so the blank should reject or undercut it, not repeat it. How far can we go? The evidence shows abbreviators know spelling and do no worse. That knocks out ‘abbreviations show bad spelling.’ It does not show texting makes spelling better: ‘at least as well’ isn’t ‘better,’ and a correlation can’t prove a cause. We need a modest answer: using these abbreviations doesn’t by itself indicate poor spelling.

choices.note: This is the popular view the linguist is arguing against. A completion that repeats the opponent’s claim after a ‘But’ is backwards.

Tempting, because it’s the opposite of the popular view. But the evidence is only that heavy texters do no worse, ‘at least as well.’ That’s not improvement, and a correlation can’t show texting causes anything. Polar opposite isn’t the logical opposite.

CORRECT. Abbreviating requires knowing the spelling, and heavy abbreviators spell at least as well as others. So abbreviation use alone isn’t evidence of weak spelling. It’s exactly as strong as the evidence allows.
We don’t know this. Heavy users score at least as well as rare users; that doesn’t mean rare users score poorly. Both groups might score well.
Unsupported comparison. Abbreviating requires knowing the full word, but nothing says it’s harder than writing the full word.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, seagrass meadows along the Sarne Coast have shrunk most sharply near the coast’s three desalination plants, which discharge a warm, highly salty brine into nearby waters. Seagrass is known to be harmed by unusually salty water. So the increased salinity of the water near the plants is probably the main cause of the meadows’ decline there.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Seagrass meadows farther from the plants have also shrunk over the past decade, though by much smaller amounts.
The three desalination plants were built on stretches of coast where the seagrass meadows had been unusually extensive.
Seagrass is also harmed by water that is much warmer than usual, and the brine raises water temperatures near the plants.
Near a coastal power station that discharges warm but not salty water, the seagrass meadows have not shrunk.
The number of boats anchoring along the Sarne Coast, whose anchors can tear up seagrass, has grown over the past decade.
questions.explanation: The brine is both warm and salty, so the shrinkage could be due to heat rather than salt; D shows that warm water alone leaves seagrass unharmed, which rules out the rival and supports salinity. C is the trap: it fits the idea that the plants are to blame, but it names heat as a competing cause and so weakens the claim about salinity.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Increased salinity near the plants is probably the main cause of the meadows’ decline there.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Meadows shrank most near the plants; the plants discharge warm, salty brine; salty water harms seagrass.

breakdown.analysis: Read the conclusion closely. It doesn’t just blame the plants. It blames the salt. But the brine is warm too. What if the heat is doing the damage? Then the plants are guilty, but the salinity claim is wrong. Strengthen by ruling out that rival: show that warm water without salt doesn’t hurt seagrass. It’s like blaming the spice, not the temperature, for a burned tongue: you test it by serving the dish hot but unspiced. We need an answer that isolates salinity from heat.

choices.note: If meadows everywhere are shrinking, something coast-wide may be at work. That gives a rival cause rather than support. At best it does nothing.
So? Bigger meadows near the plants might just have more to lose. This doesn’t link the loss to salt, and if anything hints at another explanation.
Tempting, because it makes the plants look even more harmful. But the argument blames salinity specifically. This makes heat a competing cause, which weakens that claim.
CORRECT. Warm water without salt leaves seagrass alone. That knocks out heat as the explanation, leaving the salty part of the brine as the likely culprit.
This adds a rival cause (anchors), and we aren’t told the boats cluster near the plants. It doesn’t help the salinity explanation.

questions.stimulus: In the town of Corlay, households that own a dog report knowing, on average, twice as many of their neighbors by name as households without a dog report knowing. Walking a dog brings people into frequent, casual contact with the neighbors they pass. So owning a dog leads people to become acquainted with more of their neighbors.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Corlay dog owners who walk their dogs several times a day know more neighbors by name than those who rarely do.
Some households in Corlay that do not own a dog report knowing nearly all of their neighbors by name.
Corlay residents who own cats report knowing about as many of their neighbors as do residents who own no pets.
In surveys, Corlay dog owners describe their neighborhoods as friendlier than residents without dogs describe theirs.
Most of Corlay’s apartment buildings, whose residents seldom know their neighbors by name, forbid tenants to keep dogs.
questions.explanation: E shows that households without dogs are concentrated in apartment buildings where people seldom know their neighbors for reasons that have nothing to do with dogs, so where people live, not dog ownership, may explain the gap. A is the trap: more walking going with more acquaintances fits the argument’s mechanism and so strengthens it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Owning a dog leads people to become acquainted with more of their neighbors.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Dog-owning households know twice as many neighbors by name; dog walking brings casual contact with neighbors.

breakdown.analysis: Dog owners know more neighbors. Is the dog the reason? Ask how dog owners differ from everyone else. Maybe they live in different kinds of places. If the non-owners are mostly people in buildings where nobody knows anybody, the comparison is rigged before any dog gets walked. Weaken by showing the two groups differ in some other way that explains the gap. Correct weaken answers often work like this: indirectly, through the comparison group.

choices.note: Tempting, because it’s about dogs and neighbors. But more walks going with more acquaintances fits the walking mechanism perfectly. That’s a strengthener.
‘Some’ households is nothing. An average can hide plenty of exceptions; a few friendly dogless households don’t touch the comparison.
If cats don’t help, maybe it’s the walking, not pet ownership in general. That fits the argument; it doesn’t weaken it.
Feeling that a neighborhood is friendly is a different thing from knowing neighbors by name, and it’s consistent with the dog causing it anyway.
CORRECT. Dogless households are disproportionately apartment dwellers, and apartment dwellers seldom know their neighbors anyway. Housing, not dogs, could explain the gap.

questions.stimulus: Velda Bank’s annual report notes that last year each of the bank’s five branches increased the average size of the home loans it issued, compared with the year before. The bank’s chief economist concludes that the average size of all the home loans that Velda Bank issued last year must have been larger than it was the year before.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the chief economist’s argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: takes for granted that the bank’s branches issue home loans to customers who live in the same parts of the region
presumes, without providing justification, that a larger average loan size indicates that the bank’s lending has become riskier
infers that each branch increased its total lending from the fact that each branch increased its average loan size
fails to consider that a larger share of last year’s loans may have come from branches whose loans are smaller
treats a change in the average size of loans as if it were a change in the total number of home loans the bank issued
questions.explanation: A bank-wide average depends on how loans are spread across branches; if lending shifted toward branches with smaller loans, every branch’s average could rise while the overall average fell. D names this. E is tempting because it mentions averages, but the economist never draws any conclusion about the number of loans.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The bank’s overall average home-loan size must have risen last year.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Each of the five branches raised its own average loan size.

breakdown.analysis: Sounds airtight: every part went up, so the whole went up. But averages don’t add up that way. Worked example: Branch 1 makes big loans, Branch 2 small ones. Year one: 9 loans at Branch 1 averaging $300k, 1 loan at Branch 2 at $100k. Overall average: $280k. Year two: Branch 1 makes 1 loan at $310k, Branch 2 makes 9 at $110k. Both branch averages rose, but the overall average is $130k. The mix shifted toward the small-loan branch. We need an answer that points to a change in where the loans came from.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Where customers live doesn’t affect how branch averages combine into a bank-wide average.
The economist says nothing about risk. This describes an assumption the argument never makes.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our patients are older this year, so our hospital must be doing a worse job.

choices.note: The argument doesn’t claim anything about total lending at each branch. It only reasons from branch averages to an overall average.
CORRECT. This is the mix problem. If more of the loans came from branches with smaller loans, the overall average can fall even though every branch’s average rose.
Tempting, because it’s about averages. But the conclusion is about average size, not the number of loans. The argument never confuses the two.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our average sale grew, so we must have made more sales.

questions.stimulus: All of the films nominated for this year’s Brennan Prize are documentaries. About half of the films shown at this year’s Leland Festival are documentaries. And some of this year’s documentaries received funding from the National Arts Council. So some films that received Arts Council funding were nominated for the Brennan Prize, and some were shown at the Leland Festival.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Every member of the chess club also belongs to the math club, and most members of the math club are seniors. So most members of the chess club are seniors, and so are some members of the math club.

All of the restaurants on Pine Street serve vegetarian dishes, as do about half of those in the harbor district, and some restaurants serving vegetarian dishes won a city health award. So some award winners are on Pine Street, and some are in the harbor district.

All of the paintings in the museum’s east gallery are oil paintings, and about half of those in its west gallery are. Every oil painting in the museum is insured. So all of the east gallery’s paintings and at least half of the west gallery’s paintings are insured.

Some of the volunteers at the animal shelter are teachers, and some of the teachers in town donate money to the shelter. So some of the shelter’s volunteers donate money to the shelter, and some of its donors are teachers.

All of the novels on this year’s prize shortlist were written in English, as were about half of the novels in the town library. So about half of the novels in the town library are on this year’s prize shortlist.
questions.explanation: The original has all A are C, about half of B are C, some C are D, and concludes that some D are A and some D are B, ignoring that the C’s that are D might be neither A nor B. B repeats this exactly. C has the same opening but is valid because every C is insured, and D commits a different ‘some–some’ error with only two groups.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Some Arts Council–funded films were Brennan nominees, and some were shown at Leland.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: All Brennan nominees are documentaries; about half of Leland films are documentaries; some documentaries got Arts Council funding.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: All A are C; about half of B are C; some C are D; so some D are A and some D are B.

breakdown.analysis: Where’s the gap? ‘Some documentaries’ got funding, but which ones? They could be documentaries that were neither nominated nor shown at Leland. There are lots of documentaries in the world. ‘Some’ isn’t ‘all’: the members you care about could be the other ones. This is an overlap fallacy: two groups each overlap with C, and some C have a feature, so we’re told both groups get the feature. We need the same three-part setup with a ‘some’ link and a double conclusion.

choices.note: A different flaw. This one passes ‘most’ through an ‘all’ link: chess club members could be the non-senior minority of the math club. It has no ‘some C are D’ step feeding a double conclusion.

CORRECT. All Pine Street restaurants serve vegetarian (all A are C); about half of harbor restaurants do (half B are C); some vegetarian-serving restaurants won (some C are D); so some winners are on Pine Street and some in the harbor district. Same pattern, same flaw: the winners could be vegetarian-serving restaurants on neither street.

Tempting. The first two sentences match the original almost word for word. But then it says EVERY oil painting is insured, not ‘some.’ That makes the argument valid. You can’t match a flawed argument with a valid one.

Flawed, but differently. Its first conclusion links two groups through one ‘some–some’ overlap with teachers (the second conclusion is fine). The original has three groups, and its trouble comes from an ‘all’ and a ‘half’ feeding into a ‘some.’
A different flaw. It treats sharing a trait (written in English) as membership in the shortlist. There’s no ‘some C are D’ step at all.

questions.stimulus: Westbury school district policy: A student may be excused from the physical education requirement only if a parent or guardian submits a written request for the exemption, and only if either the student has a physician’s note documenting a medical condition that makes participation unsafe or the student is a member of a school-sponsored sports team that practices at least four days a week.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the policy stated above?
choices: Lena’s mother submitted a written request, and Lena plays on the school’s volleyball team, which practices five days a week. So Lena must be excused from the physical education requirement.
Omar has a physician’s note documenting that his asthma makes participation unsafe, though no written request has been submitted for him. Since his need is documented, Omar may be excused.
Priya’s father submitted a written request, and Priya swims on a private club team that trains six days a week. So Priya may be excused from the physical education requirement.
Theo’s guardian submitted a written request, but Theo has no physician’s note, and his school cross-country team practices only three days a week. So Theo may not be excused.
Mira’s mother submitted a written request, and Mira has a physician’s note documenting a knee injury that makes participation unsafe. But she is on no school team, so she may not be excused.
questions.explanation: The policy states only necessary conditions: a written request, plus either a physician’s note or a school team practicing four or more days a week. Theo has neither a note nor a qualifying team, so the policy rules out excusing him, as D says. A is the attractive trap: Lena meets every necessary condition, but the policy never says meeting them guarantees an exemption, so ‘must be excused’ does not follow.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Excused → (written request) AND (physician’s note OR school-sponsored team practicing 4+ days a week).

setup.label: Application
setup.text: Find the judgment the policy actually supports. Since the policy lists only requirements, it can prove a student may NOT be excused (a requirement fails), but it can never prove a student must or may be excused.

breakdown.analysis: Read ‘only if’ carefully. Both conditions are necessary, not sufficient. Contrapositive: no written request → not excused; no note AND no qualifying team → not excused. So the safest conforming judgment denies an exemption to someone who fails a requirement. Check each student: Does a request exist? Is there a note, or a school team with 4+ practice days? A right answer must show a student failing one of those and conclude ‘may not be excused.’

choices.note: Tempting. Lena meets every requirement: request, school team, five days. But meeting necessary conditions doesn’t guarantee anything. The policy never says who must be excused. ‘Must’ goes too far.
Omar fails the written-request requirement. The policy says no request → not excused, so concluding he may be excused contradicts it.
Priya’s team is a private club, not school-sponsored, and she has no note. She fails the ‘either’ condition, so the policy points toward denying her, not excusing her.
CORRECT. Theo has the request, but no note, and his school team practices only three days. He fails the ‘either ... or’ requirement, so under the policy he may not be excused.

Mira satisfies the ‘or’ through her physician’s note; she doesn’t also need a team. Denying her because she’s not on a team misreads ‘either ... or’ as ‘both.’ The policy gives no ground for that denial.

questions.stimulus: Literary historian: Late in her career, the novelist Edda Raske published three novels under the name ‘J. Halloran,’ and her authorship of them was not revealed until after her death. Critics at the time praised the Halloran novels far more warmly than the novels Raske was publishing under her own name in those same years. So Raske’s late reputation suffered from critics’ bias against her, not from any weakness in her writing.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the literary historian’s argument depends?
choices: Most of the critics who reviewed Raske’s late novels disliked her personally and said as much in their published reviews.
Raske’s early novels were praised by critics at least as warmly as the Halloran novels were later praised.
No other novelist of Raske’s time used an assumed name to avoid critics’ bias.
The Halloran novels sold more copies than the novels Raske published under her own name during those years.
The Halloran novels were not substantially better written than the late novels Raske published under her own name.
questions.explanation: The historian credits the warmer praise for the Halloran novels to bias against Raske’s name, which requires ruling out the obvious alternative that the Halloran books were simply better; E does that, and negating it wrecks the argument. A is the attractive trap: personal dislike would support the historian, but the argument doesn’t need most critics to have disliked her or said so.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Raske’s late reputation suffered from critics’ bias against her, not from weak writing.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Critics, not knowing Halloran was Raske, praised the Halloran novels far more than her own-name novels from the same years.

breakdown.analysis: Same author, same years, different name, warmer reviews. Bias, right? Only if the books were about equally good. What if the Halloran novels were just better books? Then the critics were judging fairly, and the warm reviews had nothing to do with the name. The argument needs to rule that out. We need a defender: the Halloran novels weren’t substantially better written than her own-name ones.

choices.note: Tempting, because it would support the bias story. But the argument doesn’t need most critics to dislike her, let alone say so in print. Bias can be quiet and partial.
choices.negation: It is not the case that most of the reviewing critics disliked her personally and said so.

choices.note: Irrelevant. How her early novels were received says nothing about why the late ones were judged differently.
choices.negation: Raske’s early novels were praised less warmly than the Halloran novels were.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether others used pen names has no bearing on why Raske’s two sets of books were reviewed differently.
choices.negation: Some other novelist of the time used an assumed name to avoid critics’ bias.

choices.note: Sales are a different dimension from critical praise. The argument is about reviews, not the market.
choices.negation: The Halloran novels did not sell more copies than her own-name novels.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the Halloran novels were substantially better written. Then the warmer praise is explained by quality, and the bias conclusion collapses.
choices.negation: The Halloran novels were substantially better written than her own-name late novels.
